Is it enough to do the right thing yourself?

Parshas Nitzavim-Vayelech
Print PDF

In this week’s parsha, Moshe Rabbeinu says that the “revealed things” are for us. What does this mean? Rashi explains that when something not good is done out in the open, it becomes our responsibility to take care Yid does matters to every other Yid.

It’s not enough to say, “I’m doing fine.” Even if you learn Torah, do mitzvos, and behave the way Hashem wants, your job isn’t finished! You are connected to other Yidden. You have the power—and the responsibility—to help them do the right thing, too.

Which choice fits the message of this week’s parsha?

As long as I’m doing the right thing, that’s good enough.

What other people do matters to me. I can help them do the right thing, too.

The revealed things are for us and for our children.

Rashi: To get rid of any evil that’s among us.

But how do you help others do the right thing? Chayolim, this is done by showing and explaining that there is a Creator of this world: Hashem. He made every single detail, and He takes care of all of us, too.

For example, when you stop and make a Bracha before taking a drink, you show that Hashem is the one Who gives us everything we have and need.

And when you live this way, others will take notice! When you speak about Hashem naturally and behave as the Torah says, you influence the people around you. They’ll see how wonderful it is to be in Hashem’s Army, and they, too, will want to behave as a Tzivos Hashem soldier. This is how you take care of the “revealed [not-good] things” and add more light to the entire world.

Why does Hashem make Yidden responsible for one another? And are there better or worse ways to influence each other?

How can saying a bracha help remind someone about Hashem?

What is one small way you can positively influence another Jewish child this week?

Start by saying something about yourself, for example, “I know Perek Alef Tanya by heart.”

Count every third letter to find out how the Torah

Now someone else at the table who also knows that perek says “me.” You just made a connection! (If no one knows that specific perek, then someone who knows a different perek, or even a few lines, can also say “me”.) views all Yidden.

That person goes next. They could say something like, “yellow is my favorite color.”

Then someone else, who agrees,

Keep going around until everyone’s seen how all Yidden are connected.

The Long Search

Parshas Nitzavim-Vayelech
Print PDF

Our aunt traveled all the way to Tzfas to find a hidden kever, but no one knew where it was.

Growing up, our aunt Nechama often heard stories about her great-great-uncle, Ezra Chaim HaKohen. He was a well-known mekubal, and many miracles happened through him.

When she went to Eretz Yisroel a few years ago, she really wanted to daven by his kever. No one in the family knew where he was buried, so she called a historian in Tzfas named David.

“I can help you look for the kever,” he told her. “Let’s meet after Simchas Torah.”

But on that Simchas Torah—October 7th—there was a big attack in Eretz Yisroel. Our aunt had to go home without finding the kever.

Two years later, our aunt returned to Eretz Yisroel with her husband, our uncle. She contacted David again, who said he could meet her in Tzfas on Sunday.

“Call me on Friday to confirm,” he told her.

From Friday through Sunday morning, she tried calling again and again, more than thirty times! But there was no answer.

Still, they went to Tzfas.

The entire drive there felt uncertain. Everything depended on David, who wasn’t answering his phone.

When they arrived, they walked through the streets, asking if anyone knew David. Finally, a Chabad Chassid at a tefillin stand said he had seen David earlier that day. He tried calling him, but there was still no answer.

Someone nearby suggested calling a woman with the same last name as Ezra Chaim HaKohen. They called, but she didn’t know where he was buried, but she gave them the number of a man named Eli, who worked at the cemetery.

Our aunt called him. “I’ll see what I can do,” Eli said, and then he hung up.

Our aunt and uncle asked around if anyone else knew him or had seen him, and some people did! So wherever they were told he had been that day, our aunt and uncle went there to try and track him down! Hours passed, and it was getting

Should we just give up? She wondered. But then, she knew what to do. She took out her phone and began to write a letter to the Rebbe, asking for a bracha to find the kever, and emailed it into the ohel.

Just a few minutes later, her phone rang.

It was Eli. “Meet me at the Arizal’s kever,” he said.

When they arrived, Eli led them to a hidden part of the cemetery. He explained that many talmidei chachamim were buried in caves, and over time the earth had shifted, hiding many kevarim.

“What hashgacha pratit,” he said. “I don’t usually answer my phone when I’m working, but I answered your call. Then, when you said the name, I knew right away which kever you meant, because I had just been there. And I’m the only person here who knows that he’s buried in this cave!”

He brought them inside, and there it was:

the kever of Ezra

Chaim HaKohen.

Our aunt said

Tehillim by the kever, her heart everything had felt hopeless, she turned to the Rebbe—and the Rebbe’s brachos helped her finally finish her long search.

Introduction - Part 1: Army Divisions

Parshas Nitzavim-Vayelech
Print PDF

HASHEM’S ARMY DIVISIONS

Hashem’s army also has divisions. Four, to be exact. Can you remember where the Torah describes the Yidden as being divided into four?

Let’s go back in time. The shevatim had gone down to Mitzrayim, and their father, Yaakov, was about to pass away. “Promise me that I won’t be buried in Mitzrayim!” he instructed, “Instead, bring my body to Me’aras Hamachpeila in Chevron.” Then, he told his twelve sons how to carry his aron when the time comes: “You should travel as four divisions. Each division should be made up of three shevatim and hold a different side of my aron. Yehudah, Yissachar, and Zevulun, you will hold the eastern side of the aron. Reuven, Shimon, and Gad, you will carry the southern side. Efraim, Menashe, and Binyamin, you’ll be on the west, and Dan, Asher, and Naftali you’ll go on the north.” And so it was; the shevatim faithfully did as their father instructed.

Fast forward almost 200 years. The Jewish nation—Tzivos Hashem—now numbered in the millions, and it was finally time for them to leave Mitzrayim. How did they travel and camp throughout the midbar? It was all done in groups of shevatim, the very same way that they carried Yaakov Avinu’s aron! There were four divisions, one on each side of the mishkan, and the same three shevatim were placed on each side. This time, however, instead of each shevet being one person, they numbered tens of thousands!

So how did the crowds know where to be? To help them, each shevet had its own flag and each division had its own flag— totalling 12 shevet flags and 4 division flags. Each shevet’s flag displayed a unique color and symbol from the Torah, and each division flag had one of the following symbols: a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle. When you saw your flag, you knew that you were in the right place!

EVERY ARMY DIVISIONS

Every army has different divisions. For example: the ground forces battle on land, the air force fights from the skies, the navy takes control of the seas, and the intelligence collects information about the enemy.

They all work together to win the war!

Tishrei is around the corner… which means it’s time for the exclusive Tzivos Hashem Lulav & Esrog Campaign! In last year’s Hachayol (#620), we read about Reb Yisroel Jacobson, a devoted Lubavitcher chassid who brought Yanover esrogim to America, a mission that led to the z’chus of supplying the Frierdiker Rebbe and the Rebbe with a personal esrog and lulav each year, as well as the healing of a family member. His family continues this special mission today, making these esrogim available for everyone.

Hello Chayolim! My name is Rabbi Leibel Altein, as we enter the 100th year of bringing Yanover esrogim to America, I want to share a special story about my zeide, Reb Yisroel Jacobson, and the esrogim he brought for the Rebbeim.

When the Frierdiker Rebbe arrived in America in (1940), my zeide had the privilege of supplying him with Yanover esrogim for Yom Tov. Yanover esrogim, which come from Italy, are a specific type of esrog that Chabad chassidim are careful to use. My zeide had the honor of importing and selecting the esrogim to present to the Frierdiker Rebbe and Rebbe.

Then, during the 1950s, Rabbi Mordechai Perlov, a Lubavitcher rov in Milan, informed the Rebbe that a serious issue had developed.

Until then, the esrogim in Italy had grown in wild fields. But as demand increased, local farmers realized that esrogim had become valuable and began planting their own orchards. In order to strengthen the delicate fruit, they grafted esrog trees with lemon or orange trees. Grafting involves attaching a branch from one type of tree onto another until they grow together. Once grafted, the fruit is no longer considered a kosher esrog.

Esrog Agents

The story of the Yanover esrogim - part II

At first, my father, Reb Mordechai Altein, traveled with my zeide to Italy to help with the inspections. The work was difficult. Esrogim grow on thorny bushes, and they would crawl underneath them, digging down to the roots to make sure there was no evidence of grafting.

Every summer, the Rebbe would give him five one-hundred-dollar bills and one single dollar bill to help cover expenses. This continued every year until (1991).

In the early 1960s, my father was no longer able to travel with my grandfather. The Rebbe therefore instructed Rabbi Moshe Lazar, a shliach living in Milan, to join him in cutting the esrogim. Rabbi Lazar later described many times how carefully they performed this work together.

This arrangement continued until 1969, when my zeide suffered a severe heart attack and doctors told him he could no longer fly. My father then took over the responsibility and continued working with Rabbi Lazar every year.

Along with the esrogim, our family also brought lulovim to the Rebbe. My brother-in- law, Reb Yitzchok Meir Gurary of Montreal, would spend days searching through Manhattan wholesalers to find the finest lulovim for the Rebbe.

Knowing that the Rebbe preferred larger esrogim, they carefully set aside especially beautiful ones in designated boxes.

Even though the Rebbe was technically a partner in the business, he always paid for his esrogim himself using one-hundred-dollar bills. Operation Tzivos Hashem - Joining the Ranks

Parshas Nitzavim-Vayelech
Print PDF

Baila Brikman

Joining the Ranks Operation Tzivos Hashem

Was there ever something that you really wanted to do, but it felt impossible? Something that seemed so easy for other people but so hard for you? That’s how our school felt about joining Tzivos Hashem. We knew that other schools had exciting rallies and great base commanders. Their students could complete their missions and go up in rank, earn cool prizes and medals, and join Chidon. But our school wasn’t part of any of that. We’re far away in Brazil, and joining Tzivos Hashem seemed way too complicated.

Personally, though, our family signed up on our own. We did our missions online, but that was it. No rallies, no excitement in school, and no sense of doing it together. We wished that the whole school could join, but couldn’t figure out how. Then, one day, our friend’s mother, Mrs. Sigal, finally did! “I want my kids to feel more chayus when they do mitzvos,” she told our mother. “And I want them to feel more connected to the Rebbe. I will find a way for our school to join!” So she got to work. The first thing we needed was a base commander. It’s a big job that comes with many different responsibilities: leading rallies; helping with missions, promotions, and programs; and communicating with teachers, students, parents, and Tzivos Hashem HQ to make sure everything runs smoothly. But here’s the challenge: Most people in Brazil speak only Portuguese, but a base commander must also speak English. Mrs. Sigal knew that most of the English speakers in our school were busy shluchos, so finding the right person wouldn’t be easy. What would we do? Without a base commander, we couldn’t have Tzivos Hashem! One day, our amazing mother (who is a native English- speaker from Australia) made a bold decision. “I’ll be the base commander,” she told Mrs. Sigal. Even though Mommy was quite busy herself, she decided to do it as a z’chus for our bubby, who wasn’t well, and later, she continued in Bubby’s honor.

Now we could finally begin! Mrs. Sigal, our mother, and other staff members got to work putting everything into place. They showed everyone how to fill out their missions, made it super exciting to join the rallies, and arranged for the prizes and medals to reach us all the way in Brazil. But it wasn’t simple. There were still many differences between our school and other Tzivos Hashem bases. We didn’t let that stop us, and instead, found creative ways to make it all work. One challenge was the language. Our mother tried translating the rallies into Portuguese, but it was hard because she isn’t totally fluent yet. Instead, she asked students who know English to help translate. (In fact, one time, on our mother’s birthday, our six- year-old sister announced, “Mommy, I give you a bracha to speak perfect Portuguese, so that you can translate the rallies all by yourself!” We all laughed. That was what she wanted most!) Another challenge was the calendar. The seasons in Brazil are opposite the ones in half of the world. For some parts of the year, schools in America are open and Tzivos Hashem campaigns are running at full force. So while they’re all busy memorizing Tanya, learning niggunim, and fighting V’halachta Bidrachav battles, we aren’t even in school; it’s our summer break! But of course, we don’t want to miss out, so we instead learn everything during our winter months (when American kids are on their summer break). Baruch Hashem, our entire school is proud to be part of Tzivos Hashem. When Chidon started this past year, every single student who was able to participate, did! Kids from our school made it to the game show finale in New York—and some of us even won trophies!

Music blasted, Tzivos Hashem flags waved, and the boys even performed with a marching band! General Shimmy first led a special rally just for us, and then, at a Tzivos Hashem-themed lunch, he farbrenged with us, sharing uplifting stories and powerful messages. We even got to play soccer together! (And boy, is General Shimmy an excellent goalie!) After he left, each of us got a special gift: a picture magnet showing each chayol receiving rank medals from him. We still have them hanging on our fridge at home, and so do all our friends! The magnets remind us of those two special days spent with General Shimmy and the excitement he gave us to keep fighting our Yetzer Hara and continue on as a proud Tzivos Hashem base. Today, every one of the 70 children in our school who are eligible to join participates in Tzivos Hashem! We cheer each other on, work hard on completing our missions, and feel so proud to be part of Hashem’s Army. It’s hard to believe that not so long ago, it had all seemed truly impossible. It wasn’t easy, because all the Chidon books and tests are in English. But that didn’t stop us! What Can You Give Hashem?

Rosh Hashana
Print PDF

On the day a king is crowned, trumpets are blown and everyone celebrates. The loud sounds announce that this king is the ruler. On Rosh Hashana, when we blow the shofar, we’re doing exactly that: We are crowning Hashem as King—over ourselves, and over the entire world!

That’s why we also blow the shofar every day of Elul. Each blast helps us prepare ourselves to accept Hashem’s rulership; not just for the one day of Rosh Hashana, but for every day of the year.

But here’s an important question: When you crown a king, you usually bring him gifts. So what kind of gifts can we possibly bring to Hashem?

Hashem doesn’t need money, food, or fancy objects. What brings Him pleasure are the Torah and mitzvos that we do.

What is the best present to give Hashem on Rosh Hashana?

Something expensive or impressive.

Torah and mitzvos done with excitement and simcha.

With trumpets and the shofar’s sound, raise your voices before the King, Hashem.

Fill your day with learning Torah, saying pesukim, and doing mitzvos with chayus and joy. Every time you do even one of those things, you are giving Hashem the most wonderful gift. These gifts give Him tremendous nachas and pleasure, and He gives even greater gifts back to you and all of Klal Yisroel.

The most important gift of all is preparing yourself to live the year in the right way, with Hashem as the focus of your life; your King.

And when Yidden everywhere crown Hashem together, that brings the greatest bracha of all— the coming of Moshiach!

Why do we blow the shofar on Rosh Hashana if we’ve already done it throughout the whole month of Elul?

The Rebbe says that the best gifts for Hashem are Torah and mitzvos done with chayus and joy. Why does it matter how we do our avodah? Isn’t just doing it good enough?

What is one way you can show Hashem that you accept Him as your King this year?

One person starts by saying a small gift that they can give to Hashem, choosing something realistic and doable. Then they say “Our gift to Hashem is making sure to kiss the mezuzah.” The next person says the first gift plus adds on their own. “Our gift to Hashem is making sure to kiss the mezuzah AND bentching with extra kavana.” The next person continues: “Our gift to Hashem is making sure to kiss the mezuzah, bentching with extra kavana AND helping Mommy clear the table.” Keep playing until only one person can remember all of the gifts. Then when the game ends, make sure to keep all of your mini-hachlatos!

Ever got a grumpy gift? It doesn’t feel good to receive something that someone isn’t happy to give! To get through this maze, only go through a path of simcha and chayus—the way Hashem wants to receive our Rosh Hashanah gifts!

These chayolim of all different ages are excited to increase their Shabbos Mevorchim quota as a gift to Hashem for the new year—but their ribbons got all mixed up. Can you figure out which chayol is saying which kapitelach of Tehilim?

The Trip to the Ohel

Rosh Hashana
Print PDF

When our baby cousin became very sick, everyone davened for a miracle.

“Mazel tov!” Mommy said happily. “You have a new baby cousin. A girl!”

We were all so excited. We couldn’t wait to meet her!

Mommy told us that our new cousin, Sarah Leah, was born five weeks early. Baruch Hashem, she was healthy and able to go home with her family.

But three weeks later, Sarah Leah’s temperature suddenly dropped very low. She looked pale and weak. Something was wrong.

Our aunt and uncle rushed her to the hospital. “Your baby has pneumonia and the flu,” the doctors said.

Everyone was very worried. A newborn baby is very fragile, and getting so sick is extremely dangerous.

For two long weeks, our tiny cousin lay in a special hospital bed. A machine called a ventilator helped her breathe. She was very ill, and everyone davened for a miracle.

On Yud Kislev, the Mitteler Rebbe's Chag HaGeulah, our uncle went to a farbrengen. During the farbrengen, someone asked how baby Sarah Leah was doing. With tears in his eyes, our uncle told him that she was still very sick and fighting for her life.

“Did you write to the Rebbe?” the man asked.

“Of course,” our uncle said.

“Did you go to the Ohel?”

Our uncle paused. “No,” he answered. “It’s been so hectic with our baby in the hospital.”

“You must go to the Ohel in person and daven for a bracha!” the man urged.

It was already very late at night, and our uncle was exhausted. But he decided to go anyway. At midnight, when the farbrengen ended, he drove to the Ohel.

Rebbe, he wrote, please bentch our baby to be healthy. He also added: Please give us a bracha that we should dance at her wedding when she grows up.

Inside the Ohel, he davened and read his pan. Then, he went to watch the video playing on the screen.

When he entered the video room, he froze in shock. The Rebbe was beginning a new sicha with the words

before a kallah at her wedding!

At that moment, our uncle knew that he had the Rebbe’s brachos. He left the Ohel feeling calm, sure that everything would be okay.

With tremendous nissim, baby Sarah Leah began to feel better. She came home nine days later, on Yud-Tes Kislev, the Alter Rebbe's Chag HaGeulah!

But the following week, she needed to go back to the hospital again. The doctors were concerned, but Baruch Hashem, after just a few days, Sarah Leah was ready to come home once more.

Can you guess the date this time? It was the third night of Chanukah, which is the Alter Rebbe’s second Chag HaGeulah!

It was clear how everything fit together.

The farbrengen on Yud Kislev led our uncle to go daven at the Ohel. From there, the

Rebbe’s brachos helped our cousin heal, and she came home on two special days connected to the

Alter Rebbe—from one Chag HaGeulah to the next!

Seeing such a clear answer from the Rebbe helped our aunt and uncle stay strong. They knew that the Rebbe was with their baby, helping her have a complete refuah.

In this week’s parsha, the Torah says that Hashem fed the Yidden “honey from a rock, and oil from a stone.” That sounds surprising. A rock doesn’t look like something that can give food—certainly not sweet honey or rich oil. And yet, that’s exactly what happened!

This shows how much Hashem loves Yiddishe children.

From the very first Galus, He has taken personal care of them, making sure they have everything they need both b’gashmiyus and b’ruchniyus. And because it’s the children who recognized Hashem’s care so clearly while in Mitzrayim, they were also the first to recognize Him at the Yam Suf— with singing, dancing, and thanking Hashem for his miracles.

Which choice shows real trust in Hashem?

I try hard, but still worry because I don’t see how things will work out.

He let them suck honey from a rock, and oil from the mighty part of the stone.

Today, too, Hashem takes care of every single Yiddishe boy and girl. When you remember that Hashem personally gives you everything you need b’gashmiyus and b’ruchniyus, your Avodas Hashem can feel entirely different! It becomes much easier to do what He asks of you, for He has already given you all the tools you need! And you can fulfill your mission with great simcha, knowing that He is focusing on you to complete His Grand Plan!

This simcha brings even more goodness into the world and helps bring closer the final Geulah.

How can remembering Hashem’s care make mitzvos feel happier?

Yiddishe kinder have a special connection to Hashem, and that’s why Hashem takes such good care of them. Standing by the Yam Suf, they were the ones to feel Him first. Can you find 10 sparks of holiness in places that other people might not see Him?

One year, on the night before Yom Kippur, a Chassid asked Reb Elimelech of Lizhensk if he could watch how the tzaddik does kapparos.

“Well, how do you do kapparos?” Reb Elimelech replied.

The Chassid lowered his eyes. “I’m just a simple Yid,” he said. “I hold the chicken in one hand and a siddur in the other, and I say the

Reb Elimelech nodded. “That’s exactly what I do.”

But the Chassid wasn’t satisfied. “Rebbe, for more than twenty years, I’ve come to spend Aseres Yemei Teshuva with the Rebbe. But I’ve never seen the Rebbe do kapparos. I know it must be very special.”

Reb Elimelach looked at him. “You want to see something special? Then go watch how Moshe the Innkeeper does kapparos.”

The Chassid left right away.

The Most Special Kapparos

He traveled to Moshe’s inn at the edge of a nearby town and asked if he could stay for the night.

“I’m sorry, but we don’t have any available beds,” Moshe replied. “You can stay at the inn down the road.”

“Please,” the Chassid begged. “I’m very tired. I can rest in a corner.”

Moshe hesitated, then nodded. “Alright,” he said, letting the Chassid in.

The room inside was filled with Goyishe peasants drinking mashke. But after some time, Moshe sent everyone away for the night. At last, the room was empty.

The Chassid lay down under one of the tables and waited to see what would happen.

Before morning, Moshe got up, washed his hands and quietly said the morning brachos. He then whispered to his wife, “Yentel, it’s time for kapparos. Please bring me the notebook from the shelf.”

Moshe sat down on a small stool and lit a candle. The soft light flickered across the room. Yentel brought his notebook, and he began to read through a list of all the aveiros he had done that year.

“One day I spoke lashon hara,” he said in a broken voice. “Another day, I woke up too late to daven. Another time I forgot to give tzedakah.”

As he kept reading, his voice began to shake. Tears filled his eyes and ran down his cheeks. Page after page, Moshe read and cried, until he reached the very end.

After a few moments, he called out again. “Yentel, please bring me the second notebook.”

She dutifully brought it over, and Moshe opened it up.

This notebook was different. Here, Moshe had written down every difficulty that had happened to him over the course of that year.

“One day, the peasants beat me,” he read. “Another day, my child became very sick. In the winter, we had no wood and the inn was freezing cold for many nights. Then our cow died, and we had no milk.”

His voice grew quieter with each word. When he finished, Moshe lifted his eyes toward the sky. “Hashem,” he cried out, “I know I didn’t do everything right. I promised last year that I would be better, but I wasn’t always strong enough.”

He paused, holding the notebook tightly. “But I also trusted You. I asked for a good year, and I believed that You would make that happen.”

The room was very still. “Hashem, today is Erev Yom Kippur,” Moshe continued. “It’s a time when we forgive each other.”

“So I will forgive You, Hashem, for all of the troubles that happened to me. And You, Hashem, in Your kindness, please forgive me, too.”

Moshe picked up both notebooks. He lifted them high and slowly circled them above his

He then walked over to the fireplace. After one last look at the notebooks, Moshe threw them both into the cackling fire. The notebooks burst into flames, until nothing was left but ashes.

Under the table, the Chassid lay very still. Now he understood why Reb Elimelech of Lizhensk had sent him here. He had finally seen the most special kapparos of all.

The Storm Vanished

Parshas Haazinu
Print PDF

A powerful cyclone was heading straight for our city, but we weren’t afraid.

My family is on shlichus in the tropical city of Cairns, Australia, very far from other frum families. The closest shliach lives so far away that it takes more than a whole day to drive there!

Cairns is a beautiful place. Our Chabad house is surrounded by wonders of Hashem’s world, including the ocean’s Great Barrier Reef and the leafy-green Daintree Rainforest.

But living in Cairns also means living with something dangerous: cyclones. A cyclone is a huge storm with strong winds and heavy rain. Cyclones are so powerful that they can flood houses and push trees to the ground. In other parts of the world, this type of storm is called a hurricane.

Years ago, a cyclone swept through Cairns, and many people lost their homes. Baruch Hashem, our Chabad House remained safe, and we opened our doors to Jewish families who needed somewhere to stay until they could find a new place to live.

In the month of Shvat, 5781 (2021), just before one of our big community events, we heard worrisome news: Tropical Cyclone Kimi was on its way, headed straight toward Cairns.

The whole city began to prepare. Shops closed, windows were boarded up, and many people left for safer places.

Inside of our house, though, everything felt calm. Tatty told us that he was going to write to the Rebbe for a bracha, and we knew that the Rebbe would help.

Tatty went into his office and sat down at his desk. If the cyclone comes, he thought, the streets will flood and the event will be canceled. He picked up his pen to ask for a bracha that the event should go on as planned.

Then, Tatty paused. There’s something more important than the event: I should ask that no one gets hurt.

He was about to start writing, but then he stopped again. The Rebbe’s brachos don’t have limits, he thought. With strong bitachon, he began to write: Rebbe, please give us a bracha that the cyclone shouldn’t even reach Cairns at all.

This all happened the night before the cyclone was supposed to hit. Many people in the city were worried and afraid, but we went to sleep feeling calm, confident

Just to be extra safe, we put sandbags by our doors to help keep the floodwaters out.

look outside.

amazed to see a clear, blue sky and bright, shining sun. There was no sign of the cyclone at all!

We soon heard the news that the cyclone had faded away over the water without ever reaching Cairns. Everyone was safe, and our community event took place as planned.

We were awed by the clear miracle, which showed us how the Rebbe's brachos are more powerful than nature. We saw clearly that when we turn to the Rebbe, our greatest challenges—even a mighty cyclone!—can vanish and fade away.

HASHEM’S ARMY DIVISIONS IN SHAMAYIM

Now how did the Yidden know to put those specific symbols on the division flags? Amazingly enough, they saw them on the malachim’s ruchniyus’dik flags during Matan Torah. A Mitzvah’s Reward Berditchev, Ukraine

The weary traveler to Berditchev shook his head. “No,” he said. “You cannot have my esrog. Let me continue on my way, for I must hurry home for Yom Tov.”

“But you can spend it here with us, in Berditchev,” pleaded the Chossid. “And then Reb Levi Yitzchok and our entire town will be able to fulfill the mitzvah of lulav and esrog!”

Despite the Chossid’s heartfelt pleas, the traveler refused to stay.

Word of the esrog's departure reached Reb Levi Yitzchok, who hurried to meet the traveler. “Please, consider staying with us for Yom Tov,” Reb Levi Yitzchak begged. “There is not one esrog in the entire town of Berditchev. You are our only hope!”

The traveler, determined to spend Yom Tov at home, wasn’t convinced.

Reb Levi Yitzchak’s desire to fulfill the mitzvah of lulav and esrog overcame him, and he turned to the visitor once more. “If you stay and allow us to use your esrog, you will share in my portion of Olam Haba.”

Stunned, the traveler agreed. The people of Berditchev were overjoyed.

A few hours before Yom Tov, a messenger appeared at the traveler’s inn. “I have instructions for you from Reb Levi Yitzchok,” he informed the innkeeper. “Don’t allow the traveler with the esrog inside your sukkah!” The messenger continued on his way, passing on the instructions to everyone in Berditchev.

On the first night of Sukkos, the traveler returned from shul ready to make kiddush and eat the Yom Tov seuda. But as he tried to enter the sukkah, the innkeeper blocked his way!

“Please let me in,” said the traveler. “I can’t make kiddush outside of the sukkah!”

But the innkeeper stood his ground.

The traveler had to look elsewhere for a place to eat. He walked to the neighbor’s sukkah and asked if he could celebrate Sukkos with them. To his utter bewilderment, the neighbor refused. As he continued looking for a place to make kiddush, the answer was always no.

The traveler grew suspicious. Why was everyone turning him down? He questioned some of the residents, pestering them until they revealed Reb Levi Yitzchok’s instructions.

Frustrated, he ran to Reb Levi Yitzchok, and cried, “Is this how you repay me?”

“If you disregard my promise of being with me in Gan Eden,” replied Reb Levi Yitzchok, “I will let you enter my sukkah.”

The traveler stood rooted to the spot. How could he choose? It took some moments before he concluded: fulfilling the mitzvah of sitting inside a sukkah is more important than all the rewards of Olam Haba! “I agree,” he said.

Reb Levi Yitzchok invited the traveler to eat in his sukkah. He turned to him and remarked: “I made a promise to you, and I will keep it. You will indeed get a share in my Olam Haba. But it was necessary that you should work to deserve it. Once you showed that you were willing to give up the share in order to do a mitzvah, you were able to receive this lofty reward.”

Look at the bochur on the bongo drums. Did you ever see a smile like that?

Dovid has Down syndrome. Some mitzvos—like davening in shul and sitting and learning Torah—are hard for him to do. He isn’t so different that way from other people, and his mother always tells him that Hashem chose him especially for her. We kept trying to enroll in Tzivos Hashem, but nothing seemed to work.

I'll never forget the long journey that I went through in order to join Tzivos Hashem. I have wanted to enroll for, like, forever! It's the most amazing program that helps kids connect with Hashem and bring Moshiach, and I really, really wanted to be a part of it.

But, boy, was it hard! My school doesn’t have a Tzivos Hashem base, so we had to register on our own. But when Mommy tried signing me up, she kept running into one challenge after another. First, she looked online and found a few numbers to call. But when she tried calling, she couldn’t get through to the right person.

Finally, someone texted her the correct number. But for some reason, all of her text messages, including the one with that number, were deleted … twice! When Mommy asked for the number a third time, the person who had sent it to her didn’t respond. They probably thought she was pulling a prank on them.

At that point, half a year had already passed, but we didn't give up. We knew it was just the Yetzer

Hara trying to get in the way.

And so, on my birthday, which was a Friday, Mommy took me to the

Ohel. We davened for a bracha that I should finally be enrolled in

The very next business day— Monday—something incredible happened! Mommy got a message from the very person at Tzivos Hashem whose number we had lost!

I saw you were trying to sign up, she wrote. Would you like me to help you?

“Yes!” Mommy quickly typed back. And just like that, she helped me sign up! We had been trying for months, and right after asking the Rebbe for help, everything went quickly and smoothly.

I was so excited!. I began filling out my missions every day, and I immediately saw that they were helping me to stay focused on serving Hashem.

I worked on saying brachos carefully, davening with more kavana, and doing more mitzvos during the day. Sure enough, I started earning points and moving up in rank like a real soldier. It felt so good to be part of this powerful army of kids from all over the world; all working together on the same mission: bringing Moshiach.

And the best part of all? I feel like the General of the army himself picked me to be his soldier. I’ll do everything I can to make him proud!

Focused Attacks

There’s an extremely important first step that every army takes, way before making an attack: getting to know the enemy! This includes sending spies or spying devices to find out how they fight, what weapons they have, and where they are stationed, so that you can best prepare yourself. Getting to know the enemy before you attack is called “reconnaissance”, or

“recon” for short.

In Hashem’s army, we also take time for recon.

“Preemption” is when an army is proactive, meaning they don’t wait to respond to an enemy attack, but they go out and attack the enemy first. Offense, not defense. And in Tzivos Hashem, we want to attack the Yetzer Hara before it gets to us.

In Week 2, you will learn from the best of Hashem's soldiers: our division heads. How did they outwit their enemy?

Vehalachta Bidrachav Introduction

Week 1: Reconnaissance

This includes meeting with our squad to discuss the sly tactics of the Yetzer Hara. How does the Yetzer Hara try to infiltrate (get into) our camp and win us over? What thoughts could he put into your head, what feelings can those thoughts create, and how might those feelings make you behave?

For example, if we are focusing on the southern border this month, we might discuss what the Yetzer Hara would say to you if your parents are out of town, and you want to stay up past your bedtime.

When you know the tactics of the Yetzer Hara, you can recognize an attack from him right away!

Week 2: Preemption

For example, during the months focused on the southern border, you may learn what it says in Chumash and Midrash about Sara Imeinu’s consistency.

In any army, the best way to win a battle is by making a pre-emptive strike on the enemy. Attacking the enemy before the enemy gets to attack you gives you the upper hand! We must do the same in Hashem’s army, and leave no room for the Yetzer Hara to win!

Here’s how it works:

There will be four Avos Squad meetings every month, covering the four main steps in a war, which are: getting to know enemy tactics, learning the battle strategy, making the attack, and regrouping to see how you’ve done. These four battle steps are also called reconnaissance (pronounced “rekon-isins”), precedence, attack, and evaluation.

Just like children get their genes from their parents, we all inherit ruchiniyus genes from our Avos and Imahos. These are special kochos that have been passed down to every Yid, giving us the ability to be like them.

In Week 3, you will make a battle plan of how to apply what you’ve learned from that month’s division head to be powerful soldiers of Hashem.

For example, if you are conquering the south, you can learn from Sara Imeinu’s tactic of being consistent in our avodas Hashem, and how we too can stand strong against our Yetzer Hara before he tries getting us to behave in a scattered way!

Week 4: Evaluate

After an attack, the army comes together to evaluate. This means to discuss how the attack went, and how they can do even better next time.

During the last meeting of each battle, you will discuss your squad’s hachlata from Week 3. What went well? What do we still need to work on? Is there a more powerful or effective way to fight this battle? After evaluating together, you are ready to apply what was discussed, and move on to another focused attack!

You will learn more about these steps.

For example: Month One will focus on the Yetzer Hara’s tactic of convincing us to focus only on ourselves, and how Sara Imeinu teaches us to overcome this battle and be Hashem-centered. Month Two will focus on another tactic of the Yetzer Hara, and how Avraham Avinu teaches us in the sections below.

Throughout each month, you will go through all four battle steps—one step per week—as you fight a specific tactic of the Yetzer Hara with guidance from one particular division to fight, and so on.

You can now proceed with the fight, and identify which good thoughts in your mind can create good feelings and cause good actions to win against the enemy. The Missing Donations

Parshas Bereishis
Print PDF

A huge payment for camp was due right away. Where would the money come from?

Before we moved on shlichus to Melbourne, Australia, Tatty gave shiurim at Chabad of the Upper East Side in Manhattan.

At Tatty’s final shiur before our move, he made a small farbrengen to say goodbye. Afterward, the shliach, Rabbi Krasnianski, pulled Tatty aside.

“One of my donors is inspired that you’re moving so far away on shlichus,” he said. “He decided to send your family a monthly donation for the next few years.”

Tatty felt uncomfortable. “But I don’t want to take donations away from your Chabad House,” he protested.

Rabbi Krasnianski smiled. “The more a Yid gives tzedaka, the better. Helping another shliach is a wonderful thing. You should accept it.”

Sure enough, after we moved to Melbourne, the donations began arriving each month. But after a few months, they suddenly stopped.

Tatty told Rabbi Krasnianski, who was surprised. “This donor always keeps his word,” he said. “It doesn’t make sense that he would stop the payments.”

Still, Tatty decided not to ask the donor about it.

Six years passed, and we were busy with our shlichus. Tatty worked with Rabbi Moshe Kahn at Chabad Youth, organizing programs for Jewish children, teenagers, and young adults.

One of the biggest programs that they run is Camp Gan Yisroel. Ever since the camp was founded more than fifty years earlier, it had never had its own campsite. Year after year, they had to keep renting different properties, which brought a lot of stress and challenges.

Then, after a huge fundraising campaign and many open miracles, they finally bought their very own campgrounds!

But the new property needed a lot of construction work before camp could start, and money was very tight.

One day, Tatty got a surprising phone call from Manhattan.

“Hello,” the man on the phone said. “I’m the donor’s accountant. We just discovered that for the past six years, your monthly donations were being set aside, but they never reached you. We’ll send you the full amount right away.”

Tatty couldn’t believe his ears. “How much is it?”

Tatty’s eyes widened. Right away, he remembered Rabbi Krasnianski’s words from six years earlier about helping other shluchim through tzedaka.

Without hesitation, he decided to donate the entire amount to Chabad Youth.

Tatty hurried to Rabbi Kahn’s office to tell him the exciting news.

As soon as Rabbi Kahn heard the amount, his eyes filled with tears.

“You have no idea what just happened,” he said emotionally. “This morning, I needed to pay $60,000 to continue fixing up the campgrounds, but I didn’t have the money. I felt so overwhelmed, and wrote a letter to the Rebbe asking for a bracha. And now, here you are giving me that exact amount!”

The Rebbe’s bracha had come in the quickest, most exact way possible. And it didn’t end there! Soon afterward, another donor offered to cover the remaining cost of the new campsite, and Chabad Youth’s financial situation got a lot better.

Seeing such an open miracle gave everyone tremendous chayus and bitachon. The “lost” money had arrived just when it was needed most. And now, every summer, the beautiful new campsite is filled with hundreds of children growing in Torah and mitzvos!

No Need to Worry

Parshas Noach
Print PDF

The construction costs kept going up. How would they manage?

I want to tell you an incredible story about my aunt and uncle, the Marruses, who are shluchim in Texas.

A few years ago, their house was starting to feel too small. Baruch Hashem, their family had grown, and they really needed more space to continue their shlichus.

So they decided to build an addition onto their house, carefully planning out the details to make sure they could afford it.

At first, everything went according to plan. But after a few months, the construction costs started going up. Before long, they realized something very concerning:

They didn’t have enough money to finish the project.

A close friend heard about the situation and kindly gave a donation to help. But even with that, it still wasn’t enough.

The walls remained unfinished. Piles of material lay scattered on their lawn. The construction crew wouldn’t continue without the money, and my relatives didn’t know what to do next.

Around that time, my aunt traveled to

New York for the Kinus Hashluchos. On Chof- Beis Shvat, she went to the Ohel and wrote a letter to the Rebbe.

Please give us a bracha to finish building our home in the best way, she wrote, and that we should have menuchas hanefesh even in this stressful situation.

Holding her letter, my aunt waited in the long line with many other shluchos. When it was almost her turn, she called her husband so he could say Tehillim at the same time as when she would be in the Ohel.

As soon as he got her call, my uncle stopped what he was doing. He put on his hat, jacket, and gartel, and began saying Tehillim.

After a few kapitelach, his phone suddenly rang. Usually, he wouldn’t answer in the middle of saying Tehillim. But when he saw who was calling, he picked up.

It was the same friend who had helped them before. “How’s construction going?” the friend asked.

“The price is still much more than expected,” my uncle answered honestly. “We’re really stuck.”

There was a short pause. Then his friend said, “I want to help you. I’m sending you $25,000 right now. Zei gezunt.”

My uncle sat there in shock, overwhelmed with gratitude for the clear miracle that had just happened.

A few minutes later, my aunt called. “When I was davening, I felt that everything would work out,” she told him. “There’s nothing to worry about.”

“Nothing to worry about?” my uncle exclaimed. “Let me tell you what just happened!”

He told her about his friend’s call, and she was amazed. The bracha had come at the exact moment when she had been davening at the Ohel.

“I think you should go back into the Ohel and thank the Rebbe for this special bracha,” he said.

Of course, she did just that.

What had seemed impossible moments before was now taken care of. They were finally able to finish construction, so they could continue their shlichus with enough space for their family.

This story reminds me that when we turn to the Rebbe and share what we’re going through, the Rebbe finds a way to help. And when things work out, we should report back to the Rebbe to say thank you!

Hashem promises Avraham Avinu that whoever blesses him will be blessed. Chazal teach that this also applies to all of Avraham’s children: Any time we bentch another Yid, Hashem Himself bentches us back!

In general, there are two types of brachos that a person could receive. The first kind can only be enjoyed after the person puts in effort, but with the second kind, no work is needed.

To understand this, imagine a mother who wants to give her children a special meal.

She could show them how to make the recipes, or allow them to go to the cabinets and help themselves. That's like the first kind of bracha.

Another option would be for the mother to set up the meal nicely on the table. When the children come home, they can sit down right away. They don't have to do anything except enjoy the yummy food. That's like the second kind of bracha.

When we bentch another Yid, Hashem is so happy that He gives us the second type of bracha—in great amounts and without limits!

I will bless those who bless you.

Think about it: If Hashem's brachos come to any Yid who blesses another, how much more so when soldiers in Tzivos Hashem bless other Yidden!

Everything that we chayolim do is especially precious to Hashem because our words are pure and free of aveiros. When we bentch another Yid, Hashem puts aside all of His other business— even though it’s all very important and holy!— and gets busy sending wonderful brachos to us; the second kind that we can enjoy right away.

Can you think of someone who could use your brachos?

What happens when we bentch another Yid?

The brachos go only to them.

Why do you think the tefillos of children are so precious?

Hashem also sends us brachos that need no effort.

Name some of the brachos that Hashem gives you every day.

Here’s a chance to give out brachos in real time! First, collect a bunch of random objects into a paper bag. Start by picking out an object, connecting it to a bracha, and choosing someone to bentch. Keep going until every person has a turn.

Toss a ball around the room.

Whoever catches it has 5 seconds to name one bracha they didn't earn (was a gift from Hashem). No repeats!

What would you rather—a bunch of groceries or a beautifully set supper table? Connect 5 objects in 5 different paths to show how a bracha (1 single item) can become even better.

The Missing Package

Parshas Lech Lecha
Print PDF

The mezuza cases were sent out to be finished. Why didn’t they come back?

A few years ago, Mommy organized a special Jewish women’s event in our community all about the mitzvah of mezuza. Many homes in our area didn’t yet have mezuzos, and Mommy hoped that this would inspire more women to put them up.

For the activity, everyone designed their own mezuza case using a special kit. The cases were made with glass and needed to be finished by an artist before they could be used.

The event was a big success. Everyone had a great time, and the mezuza cases came out beautifully.

Right away, Mommy mailed all the cases to the artist so she could finish them. Then, she waited for them to be returned.

But the box never arrived.

At first, Tatty and Mommy were busy and didn’t think about it too much. But after a few weeks, Mommy checked in with the artist.

“I already sent them back,” the artist said, surprised. “They should have arrived weeks ago.”

The artist gave Mommy the tracking number, and Mommy looked it up right away. “It shows that the package was delivered,” she said. “But we never got it!”

Tatty checked the cameras outside of our house to see what happened on that day, but there was no sign of any delivery.

Mommy’s heart sank. The women were waiting for their mezuza cases, and now, it looked like they were lost! But Mommy was also worried. What if people wouldn’t want to come to future events because of this mix up?

The artist kindly offered to remake all of the mezuza cases, and Mommy sent out an email to everyone, explaining what had happened. Still, it was very upsetting.

That Friday, Tatty traveled to New York for a family simcha. But before going anywhere else, he went straight to the Ohel and asked for a bracha that the mezuza cases should be found.

Less than an hour later, Mommy started getting messages from people with amazing news: A woman who worked in a nearby community had just posted a message online: I got a box for Mrs. Kornfeld. Does anyone know who that is?

It turned out that the box had been delivered to the wrong address. It had been sitting in this woman’s golf cart for over three weeks! She had gone away on vacation soon after it arrived, and only now, right after Tatty davened at the Ohel, did she try to find the owner.

Mommy quickly went to pick up the package.

Baruch Hashem, all of the mezuza cases were there, safe and sound. The women were excited to hang them up, and before long, many more homes in our community had mezuzos on their doorposts!

Tatty and Mommy told the whole community about the story. Everyone was amazed at the Rebbe’s brachos, and how he always finds a way to help.

No Evidence

Parshas Vayeira
Print PDF

The doctors didn’t think that Greg would get better. After davening at the Ohel, his test results shocked everyone.

One evening in (2021), a man from our city named Greg was driving home from work. Suddenly, an extreme pain shot down one side of his body.

He rushed to the hospital, and after many tests, the doctors had frightening news: Greg had a very serious disease.

They began strong treatments right away. But they warned Greg that the illness was already at stage four—the most dangerous stage—and most patients did not recover from it.

Everything in Greg’s life changed. He stopped going to work, sold many of his belongings, and prepared for the end of his life, which the doctors expected to happen very soon, Rachmana litzlan.

But something else changed, too. Gashmiyus things no longer mattered to Greg anymore, and he became thankful for each new day.

One day, Greg’s friend Larry called.

“My daughter is also very sick,” Larry said. “I’m flying to New York with Rabbi Mendy Lipskier, a Chabad rabbi, to daven at the Rebbe’s Ohel. Why don’t you join us?”

Greg wasn’t frum and had never heard of the Rebbe. “I don’t do things like that,” he replied.

Still, Larry encouraged him to at least have lunch with Rabbi Lipskier (our father) before deciding. Greg agreed.

During lunch, Tatty told Greg about the Rebbe, explaining how people go to the Ohel to daven for brachos and ask Hashem for a miracle.

The whole idea seemed very strange to Greg, but finally, he agreed to go.

When they arrived, Tatty encouraged Greg to take on a hachlata as a keili to receive the Rebbe’s brachos. Greg decided to put a mezuza on his door.

Tatty then helped Greg put on tefillin and showed him what to do inside the Ohel. Greg went inside and read his letter, davening for a miracle.

Even though the whole experience felt very new to him, Greg felt deeply moved.

After the trip, Greg continued the difficult treatments for many months. At one point, he was so sick that he had to stay in the hospital for a few weeks. Slowly,

Greg got stronger until he was able to go home.

At one point, the doctors told him that they would need to run two important scans to check if the treatments were working.

After the first scan, Greg and his wife went out for lunch. While they were eating, Greg’s phone buzzed with a message from the doctor: No evidence.

This meant that the doctors couldn’t find any signs of the illness!

Greg was amazed and grateful, but there was still another scan left to do. This one would check for an even more dangerous part of the illness which the first scan may not have found.

The next day, he went in for the second scan. Afterward, he and his wife stopped for lunch again, waiting nervously for the results.

His phone buzzed a second time.

Greg’s hands shook as he reached for the phone. Slowly, he looked down at the screen. No evidence.

The doctors couldn’t believe it.

Many specialists had already told

Greg that it was impossible to recover from such a serious illness. But now, the illness was completely gone!

Greg knew with complete certainty that Hashem had given him an open miracle thanks to the Rebbe’s brachos. Years after Gimmel Tammuz, we saw with our own eyes how the Rebbe continues helping Yidden in incredible ways.

What’s the Greatest

Type of Kindness?

Orders from our General

Avraham Avinu and Sara Imeinu were always excited about doing gemilus chasadim, and specifically, hachnasas orchim. When a visitor came to their door, they would hurry to prepare a delicious meal. Avraham himself would take care of his guests, ready to serve them anything they needed.

Of course, when the three malachim came, they were treated with the same honor. And do you know what Avraham and Sara were promised while they were busy helping their guests? That a son would be born to them!

From here we see that the birth of the first Yiddishe baby is connected to hachnasas orchim specifically, and to all types of gemilus chasadim, in general.

Gemilus Chasadim Check

Which kind of kindness is the most powerful?

Helping someone in a gashmiyus way.

Helping another Yid’s neshama grow through Torah and mitzvos.

Redt Tzu Kinder,

And Avraham rushed to the tent and said to Sara, "Quickly … [prepare flour;] knead and make cakes."

This teaches us an important lesson: We Yiddishe children have a special connection to gemilus chasadim.

This special mitzvah has different levels. One type of kindness is doing a favor for others—sharing a snack or toys, befriending someone who’s lonely, or letting another child go first. (Boys helping boys and girls helping girls.)

There’s also another kind of gemilus chasadim: doing a favor for our own neshama by acting in the Yiddishe way, learning Torah, and doing mitzvos. This is also a wonderful type of chessed.

This shows that the greatest kind of gemilus chasadim is when we combine both types by helping someone else’s neshama!

The lesson for us chayolim is to do all three types of gemilus chasadim. And when we do, we will help and inspire the people who we meet, until the whole world is lit up with the knowledge of Hashem!

What brought Mordechai, a Gerrer Chossid, to the Kinus Hashluchim?

The banquet hall was packed with thousands of shluchim from around the world, all joining together b’achdus. Everyone sang and danced, so proud to be the Rebbe’s shluchim on the front lines to bring Moshiach.

Soon, it was time to go. Rabbi Sholom Leverton, my teacher’s father, left the hall on a high. He was filled with new chayus and energy to continue his shlichus with even more ko’ach.

As Rabbi Leverton walked to his car, a Gerrer Chossid hurried over. “Could you give me a ride to my car?” he asked. “It’s parked a few blocks away.”

“Of course,” Rabbi Leverton said. But he was curious. “What’s your name?” he asked as he pulled out of his parking spot. “And what brought you to the Kinus?”

“My name is Mordechai,” said the man, “and I come to the Kinus every year to thank the Rebbe.”

Rabbi Leverton looked at him in surprise. “To thank the Rebbe?”

“Yes,” Mordechai said. “Let me tell you my story. A few years ago, when my wife was expecting a baby, the doctors gave us very sad news. ‘'Your baby might not survive,’ they told us, ‘'and even if he does, he could be very sick.’”

Mordechai’s voice shook as he remembered that hard time. “We were heartbroken,” he continued. “My father took me to many tzaddikim for brachos, but as the pregnancy continued, the doctors became even more convinced that the baby wouldn’t survive.”

He wiped a tear from his eye. “One day, my grandmother told me something I had never known before. She told me, ‘'When I was expecting your father, the doctors were also very worried. I went to the Lubavitcher Rebbe for a bracha, and your father was born completely healthy.’”

Mordechai continued, “My grandmother looked me in the eyes and said, '‘Mordechai, you should go daven at the Ohel.’

“I was amazed to hear about my father’s miracle. And of course, I listened to my grandmother’s words. My wife and I traveled to the Ohel and davened for a bracha.

“We also made a promise: If our baby is born healthy, we will name him Menachem Mendel.”

Rabbi Leverton gripped the steering wheel tighter. “And what happened?” he asked.

A wide smile spread across Mordechai’s face. “Unbelievably, although the doctors were so worried, our baby was born completely healthy! And just as we promised, we named him

“We’re getting ready for his upshernish now,” he continued, his eyes shining. “It’s been almost three years, and we are so grateful for the Rebbe’s bracha.”

Rabbi Leverton marveled at the clear miracle that this Gerer

Chossid had seen right after davening at the Ohel. “Did you ever bring your son to the Ohel to thank the Rebbe?” he asked.

“Of course!” Mordechai answered. “We go together as a family every Motzei Shabbos. We almost never miss a week.”

Rabbi Leverton was amazed. Mordechai wasn’t even a Chabad Chossid, but just going to the Ohel and connecting with the Rebbe there brought his family the tremendous bracha of a healthy child. How much more so for us, Chassidim of the Rebbe!

Parshas Toldos
Print PDF

Tatty and Mommy were ready for their own shlichus. But how would they know where to go?

For two years, Tatty and Mommy joined our uncle and aunt on shlichus at the University of Maryland.

They loved it! They met Jewish students, helped them learn Torah and do mitzvos, and showed them the warmth of Yiddishkeit.

Time flew by quickly, and before they knew it, the two years were almost over. It was time to find their own permanent shlichus.

So Tatty and Mommy began asking around and speaking to different people. They soon heard about four different campuses that needed shluchim. One of them was the University of South Florida—called “USF”—in Tampa, Florida.

USF sounded like a great place for them to go on shlichus. But Tatty and Mommy still weren’t completely sure.

Around Chof-Beis Shvat, (2008), Tatty went to the Ohel. He wrote to the Rebbe and asked for guidance: Which campus shlichus should we choose?

After leaving the Ohel, Tatty went into the room where the Rebbe video was playing.

It was a video from the Kinus Hashluchos in (1991). The Rebbe was saying a sicha to the shluchos in the big shul of 770.

Tatty watched quietly. Then, suddenly, he saw something that made his eyes grow wide.

There on the screen was Mommy, standing in front of the crowd!

Of course, she wasn’t Mommy yet. She was a little girl then, visiting the Rebbe with her mother, Mrs. Ruth Cohen. They had come from Leeds, England, where their family was on shlichus.

Tatty stared in shock. Wait a minute, he thought. Mommy told me that she only came to the Rebbe once as a little girl. It was for the Kinus Hashluchos in.”

And now, right after he had asked the Rebbe where they should go on shlichus, that very video was playing in front

Tatty could hardly believe it. Out of all the Rebbe videos that could have been playing, he was watching the one and only video with Mommy in it.

Tatty felt that something special was about to happen. Holding his breath, he watched

as the video continued.

After the sicha, the Rebbe began giving dollars to the shluchos. One shlucha after another passed by, but JEM had put background music, so Tatty couldn’t hear what they were saying.

Then the fifth shlucha came onto the screen. It was Mrs. Sulha Dubrowski, a shlucha from Tampa, Florida.

Just then, the background music became quieter, and Tatty could hear her words clearly. “A bracha for the institutions in Tampa, Florida,” Mrs. Dubrowski said to the Rebbe.

The Rebbe answered, “Amen.”

Then the Rebbe gave her another two dollars and said, “For the entire institution. Much success.”

Tatty stood frozen in his spot. Tampa, Florida! The very place that they were thinking about!

He understood that this was the Rebbe’s answer. The Rebbe was showing them where to go and giving a bracha for their shlichus.

And so, that summer, Tatty and Mommy moved to Tampa and started our Chabad House at the University of South Florida.

From the very beginning, we knew that our shlichus came with the Rebbe’s clear guidance and bracha. And until today, we feel the Rebbe’s brachos constantly, in every step of our shlichus.

Sometimes, we also have questions. We don’t always know which choice is right. But this story reminds us that a Chossid can always turn to the Rebbe and ask for guidance. The Rebbe is with us, and he will find a way to answer!

How Does Our Connection Become Stronger?

Parshas Vayeitzei
Print PDF

Connection Become Stronger?

When we do something three times, it becomes strong and lasting. In halacha, something done three times in a row is in a different category than something done only once or twice. And when we make a hachlata, it becomes a true part of us after we’ve kept it three times in a row.

Since Levi was Leah Imeinu's third son, he represents this idea of a chazaka. And that's why, after giving birth to him, Leah knew that she would have a stronger connection to Yaakov Avinu.

also hints to the entire Yiddishe nation and our connection to Hashem, who is sometimes called our "Husband”.

What helps a mitzvah become part of who you are?

Doing it once with lots of chayus.

Doing it again and again until it becomes a chazaka.

And [Leah Imeinu] gave birth to a son, and she said, "Now, this time, my husband will be attached to me, because I gave birth to three sons."

Therefore, He named him Levi.

How do we become more "attached" to Hashem? This happens by doing mitzvos. The special attachment between the Yidden and Hashem is a strong one, and it lasts forever.

The children of Levi also have their own special mission. The job of each Levi is to attach with, with their avodah in the Beis Hamikdash.

Shevet Levi's job teaches us an important lesson: We must help every Yid in their avodah, too. After all, every Yid is called Hashem’s Kohen! And so, just as Shevet

Levi helped the Kohanim with their holy work, every Yiddishe child must help other Yidden learn more Torah and do more mitzvos. How lucky we are to help other Yidden become more attached to Hashem!

Where else in Yiddishkeit do we find the idea of a chazaka?

What's something that you would like to make into a permanent part of your life?

How can you get friends to join you in doing mitzvos?

Go around the table, and everyone shares a way that you can become more “attached” to

Hashem. The first person starts with an Alef, then a Beis, then a Gimmel. Keep going until you’ve gone through the entire Alef-Beis!

Help attach these chayolim to mitzvos! Using their pictures as clues, draw a line between each chayol and the mitzva they match with.

Can you attach the mitzvah to its match?

The New X-Rays

Parshas Vayeitzei
Print PDF

Tatty tore up Shaya’s test results at the Ohel. What would the new ones show?

In Adar (2024), my brother Shaya’s leg hurt terribly. The pain kept getting worse, so Tatty and Mommy took him to a bone doctor.

The doctor took X-rays and studied them carefully. His face grew very serious. “These don’t look good,” he said quietly. “Shaya needs an emergency MRI.”

At first, Tatty hoped the doctor was simply being extra careful. He showed the X-rays to a radiologist friend, but the friend was also worried. “This really doesn’t look good,” he said. “Shaya may need even bigger tests.”

So Tatty and Mommy took Shaya for the MRI. The next day, the results came back: Shaya had a serious tumor in his thigh, and the doctors were very concerned.

Tatty and Mommy began to cry. “Will Shaya be okay?” they asked.

“We won’t know until we do bigger tests,” the doctors replied.

The tests were scheduled for the following week, so Tatty quickly booked flights to New York to daven at the Ohel first. Remembering the Rebbe’s advice, he brought all of our mezuzos along to be checked.

Throughout the flight, they cried, not knowing what would be. Tatty reminded Mommy of the niggun “Fort a Yiddele”, in which the Rebbe tells a Yid in danger, “You will not drown.”

“We are going to daven at the Ohel,” Tatty said. “The Rebbe will make sure that we don’t drown.”

At the Ohel, Tatty, Mommy, and Shaya each wrote a letter and davened for a long time. Before leaving, Tatty tore up copies of Shaya’s MRI and X-rays and dropped them into the pile with everyone’s letters.

“Rebbe,” he said, “please make sure Hashem tears up this entire problem and it should just go away!”

The Rebbe often told people to get a second opinion for medical problems, so Tatty searched for a top doctor and heard about one at the Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston, where we live.

The next day, Friday, Tatty called Rabbi Lazaroff, who helps many patients in Houston. “Can you help us get an appointment?” Tatty asked.

“I don’t know this doctor,” Rabbi Lazaroff replied, “but I’ll try.”

On Motzei Shabbos, Rabbi Lazaroff called back. “You won’t believe it!” he said. “One of

the families staying with us had an urgent appointment. The doctor told them, ‘'tell your rabbi that I will help his people. The office will call them on Monday.’”

Sure enough, the doctor’s office called and scheduled an emergency appointment for

Tuesday morning.

When they arrived, a nurse brought a hospital gown for Shaya. “We need to take a new X-ray,” she explained.

Shaya became upset. “We already took X-rays last week,” Mommy said.

“The doctor wants new ones,” the nurse replied.

Suddenly, Tatty felt a spark of hope. “This is how miracles start happening,” he told Mommy. “We tore up the old results at the Ohel. They’re going to find something different today.”

The doctor took new X-rays and was very happy with what she saw. “There’s no need for bigger tests,” she said. “Shaya will need extensive bone surgery to remove the tumor, but I’m confident that he will be fine.”

Tatty and Mommy almost danced with joy!

Baruch Hashem, the surgery was successful, and Shaya went home that same day. Four months later, he was walking on his own two feet, completely healthy!

Faced with a big challenge, Tatty and Mommy turned to the Rebbe and followed his guidance. And Hashem sent Shaya a miraculous refuah!

This story reminds us that when we go through hardships, we are never alone. We can always turn to the Rebbe and hold on to hope. Hashem can bring revealed good in ways we never imagined!

What’s Really Important?

Parshas Vayishlach
Print PDF

Can you imagine what it was like for Yaakov to live with Lavan for so many years? When Yaakov sent messengers to Eisav, he explained: “All this time, I lived like a stranger.” Yaakov meant that he didn’t get comfortable in Charan; he never considered Lavan’s house to be his real home.

Lavan’s house is compared to Olam Hazeh. Yaakov was hinting to Eisav that he never got comfortable with all the gashmiyus things of this world. While most people care about having lots of money or getting pleasure from nice shoes, toys, or games, Yaakov didn’t think those were important. This world was not his real home.

Instead, Yaakov cared about Torah and mitzvos. That’s how he tried to spend most of his time. Torah and mitzvos were like Yaakov’s “home”

that’s where he felt most comfortable.

Later in the parsha, the Torah tells us that Yaakov built a house for himself, but for his cattle, he made little huts, like sukkos. A sukkah is much less sturdy than a house. We see from here that Yaakov considered “himself”—his neshama and ruchniyus avodah—the priority. And his “cattle”—his wealth and gashmiyus things—were much less important.

And by putting his neshama’s needs first, Yaakov accomplished something amazing: he managed to keep the entire Torah, even while living in the home of the rasha, Lavan!

[Yaakov said,] “I lived with Lavan.”

“And I [still] kept all 613 mitzvos.”

We, too, must look at the world the way Yaakov did. When we remember that our neshama is what’s important and our gashmiyus is just there to help, we’ll be sure to change the world into a beautiful home for Hashem!

How are Yaakov's challenges in Lavan's home like the challenges we face today?

Why is it hard to make Torah and mitzvos our priority?

What does it look like to treat our neshama’s needs more important than our gashmiyus?

What is most comfortable for a Yiddishe neshama?

Having lots of fun and expensive things.

Living with Torah and mitzvos as our real home.

Yaakov kept 613 mitzvos while living with Lavan.

Yaakov built a home for himself—his neshama—and a hut for his cattle.

Signing the Lease

Parshas Vayishlach
Print PDF

Shabbos was getting closer, and Tatty still couldn’t decide. Then, the phone rang.

It was Friday morning, and Tatty looked very worried. He paced from room to room, glancing at the clock again and again. He had a big decision to make before Shabbos, and he didn’t know what to do.

You see, Tatty and Mommy run YJP of West Palm Beach, where young Jewish professionals come to learn Torah, do mitzvos, and connect to Hashem. They also run the Northwood Shul, which is a warm and welcoming minyan for all types of Yidden.

Since they didn’t have a separate place for the minyan and all the programs, everything was happening right in our house. Baruch Hashem, as more and more people joined, it was starting to feel crowded.

Now, Tatty had the chance to lease a bigger place that could welcome many more Yidden. But it cost a lot of money, and he wasn’t sure if this was the right step.

Shabbos was getting closer, and time to sign the lease was running out. Tatty still couldn’t decide.

Suddenly, the phone rang.

It was a woman from the neighborhood. “Can you please come to put up a mezuza on my door before Shabbos?” she asked. “I really don’t want it to wait.”

Tatty paused. There was so much on his mind, but helping another Yid comes first. “I’m on my way,” he said.

As he drove, his thoughts were racing. Quietly, he spoke to the Rebbe in his heart. Rebbe, please show me a sign so I’ll know what to do.

When Tatty got there, he put up the mezuza while the woman watched. Then, to his surprise, she began talking about the Rebbe.

“I listen to podcasts and stories about the Rebbe all the time,” she said. “One thing that I’ve learned is to never push off a mitzvah. When a mitzvah can be done, you do it right away. That’s why I called you so urgently before Shabbos.”

Tatty was shocked. Here he was, so unsure if he should sign the lease, and this woman was telling him what she learned from the Rebbe: never push off doing a mitzvah!

At that moment, everything became clear. If getting a bigger place would help more Yidden learn Torah and do mitzvos, then the Rebbe wants him to sign the lease right away.

Tatty hurried to sign the contract and arrived at home just twenty minutes before Shabbos. He was amazed to hear that at the exact moment when the woman shared the Rebbe’s message with him, Mommy had been writing a letter to the Rebbe, asking for guidance about this decision!

That night, as we sat around our Shabbos table, everything felt calm again. Tatty and

Mommy were no longer unsure; they knew they had made the right choice.

Baruch Hashem, our new space is full of

Yidden who come to learn, daven, and do mitzvos. And we feel so connected to our Rebbe, who helped guide Tatty at exactly the right moment.

All of Yaakov Avinu’s sons were tzaddikim. They grew up in his home, learned Torah, and behaved as righteous Shevatim should. But if they were all

The answer is that there are different levels in being a tzaddik. Doing the right thing is important— but we shouldn’t stop there. Yosef didn’t say, “I’m already good enough. I don’t need to work any harder.” He kept pushing himself to do better, and that’s why he earned the special title.

Think about your own day for a moment. You may have learned Torah, davened, and done wonderful mitzvos! But looking even more closely, you might notice that there were moments when you could have tried harder—maybe you could have learned with more chayus, focused better in davening, or helped someone with more Ahavas Yisroel. Even when you fill your day with goodness, there’s always a way to add even more.

Yosef Hatzaddik lived this way—especially when things were difficult. Most of his life was spent in Mitzrayim, surrounded by people who didn’t behave according to the Torah. Yosef was busy, important, and constantly around not- good influences. Still, he didn’t change who he was. Instead of being pulled down, he grew even stronger. Truly, Yosef Hatzaddik.

We learn this from Yosef … who is called Yosef Hatzaddik.

Let’s learn from Yosef’s example. No matter where we are, and no matter how hard things feel, we can always serve Hashem better and better. We can be like Yosef Hatzaddik: always growing and remaining proud Yidden.

I already did well, so I can take it easy now.

I already did well, and I’ll look for more ways to keep growing.

A Brocha for Children

Parshas Vayeishev
Print PDF

It was already a few years after their chasunah, and Tatty and Mommy still didn’t have any children. When would they hold a baby of their own?

On Chol Hamoed Sukkos 5775, Tatty bumped into a friend. This friend had been married for more than five years and didn’t have any children. As they spoke, his friend shared amazing news: After so many years of waiting, they finally had a baby on the way!

“It’s all thanks to the Rebbe’s brochos!” his friend said happily. “Last Lag Ba’omer, I went to the Ohel with some mekuravim from my mivtzoyim route. On the way, I discussed with them how Lag Ba’omer is a special day to go to the Ohel and daven for children. They said that they would daven for me! When we got to the Ohel, I asked the Rebbe for a brocha for children, and they davened for me as well. Soon after Lag Ba’omer, we found out that we were expecting!

“When I shared the good news with the mekuravim from my mivtzoyim route, one of them said, ‘the brocha came from Lag Ba’omer!’. Even the mekuravim realized that the brocha came from the Rebbe!”

Tatty was thrilled to hear the good news. “You know,” he said thoughtfully, “going to the Ohel on Lag Ba’omer and davening for children is important and special. But if you bring along someone else who otherwise wouldn’t go, that makes it really special!”

Tatty felt that his friend merited to have a baby because he brought along the mekuravim from his mivtzoyim route. Right then and there, he decided to do the same thing! Next Lag Ba’omer, he would take someone along with him to the Ohel and they would daven for a brocha for children. Tatty and Mommy hoped that in that zechus, they would finally merit the brocha of having a child of their own.

That year, a few days before Lag Ba’omer, Tatty called an Israeli he knew who lived in Manhattan. He shared his friend’s story and asked if he would come along with

him to the Ohel to daven for children. The man immediately agreed. When Lag Ba’omer finally arrived, Tatty picked the man up from Manhattan and drove with him to the Ohel.

They davened with all their might for a brocha for children, and that is exactly what happened. Nine months later, almost exactly to the day, on Tes Zayin Shvat 5776, I was born! You can’t imagine what a simcha it was!

I am so grateful to the Rebbe for answering Tatty and Mommy’s tefillos. We are so lucky to be chassidim of the Rebbe who cares so much about us! Let’s do as many mitzvos as we can to make the Rebbe proud!

Recon Mission

Getting to know the enemy’s weapons and tactics before planning

In a war, the first step toward victory is to expose the enemy’s strategy. This way, we avoid falling into his trap. In Tzivos Hashem we face the trickiest enemy: the Yetzer Hara.

Here’s his strategy: First, the Yetzer Hara plants negative thoughts in our heads. Then, those thoughts grow into worse feelings that can lead to even more dangerous actions.
