Rebbe Story

Case Closed

Parshas Mikeitz
Print PDF

The FBI investigation was turning the man’s life upside-down.

Our rav, Rabbi Baruch Epstein, was at a restaurant one day when a Litvisher Yid came over to him.

“Are you a Lubavitcher?” the man asked. “I must share a story with you about the Rebbe!”

He began telling Rabbi Epstein about a close friend who had been his chavrusa for many years.

It happened one day that this chavrusa discovered some alarming news: He found out that he was being investigated by the FBI. He became very worried and afraid. The FBI is a powerful government agency, and if they decided that he had done something wrong, he could face huge fines or even be sent to prison!

The worry followed him everywhere. At night, he lay awake, thinking about what might happen. And during the day, he couldn’t bring himself to relax. Would he lose all his money? Would he get into even bigger trouble?

The stress hurt his health, his parnassa, and his shalom bayis. He had so much heartache that he even stopped learning with his long-time chavrusa.

“It was so hard to see him suffer,” the man told Rabbi Epstein.

A few weeks later, the two friends met again. But the man noticed right away that something had changed. His chavrusa looked much calmer and happier.

“What happened?” he asked. His chavrusa told him the story:

Soon after they had stopped learning together, he traveled to New York to meet with a lawyer. The day before the meeting, he met an old friend and told him about his crisis with the FBI.

“You’re in New York!” the friend said. “Everyone knows that when a Yid has a problem, he goes to the Rebbe’s Ohel to ask for a bracha. You should go, too.”

At first, the chavrusa refused. He was Litvish and didn’t feel comfortable going to the Ohel.

But then he realized that the Ohel was actually quite close to the lawyer’s office in Long Island. It couldn’t hurt to stop there on the way. He decided to give it a try.

While at the Ohel, he was surprised to see someone he knew from the Litvisher Ponevezh Yeshiva. “What are you doing here?” he asked.

The other man smiled shyly. “I also came to ask for a bracha.”

Now the chavrusa felt more comfortable. He saw that he wasn’t the only Litvisher Yid who had come to the Rebbe’s Ohel.

After davening for a bracha, he drove to the lawyer’s office and explained the difficult situation.

The lawyer listened to the whole story. Then, he picked up the phone and called the people he knew at the FBI.

The chavrusa sat there, his heart pounding. What would they say?

It wasn’t long before he was given shocking news: The FBI wasn’t really after him! They only thought that he might know information about someone else. After a few more questions, they closed his case!

The chavrusa could hardly believe it. The frightening investigation that had been turning his life upside-down was suddenly over!

“From that moment on,” the man told Rabbi Epstein, “my chavrusa’s life started getting back to normal. He felt better, things at home became calmer, and we were able to learn together again.”

When I heard this story, it felt very powerful to me. During one of the hardest times in this man’s life, he went to the Ohel, and the Rebbe helped him in such a clear way.

The Rebbe is the Rosh Bnei Yisroel, the head of all Yidden. It doesn’t matter what path a Yid follows or what group he belongs to; when a Yid is in pain and turns to the Rebbe, the Rebbe feels his pain and finds a way to help.

Battle At the River

Parshas Mikeitz
Print PDF

The popular niggun of “Didan Notzach” was composed in (1986), during the court case of the sefarim. These powerful words mean “Victory is ours!” But did you know these words are actually much older than that? They come from a fascinating midrash about a holy man named Abba Yosi and the village of Tzitor. During the celebrations of Hey Teves, (1987), the Rebbe explained that this story teaches every Yid how to defeat the Yetzer Hara.

THE the sefarim. These powerful words mean “Victory is ours!”

Little Avrahami felt like an adult. For the first time, his father had allowed him to join the men of Tzitor on an important mission. It was still before dawn as they walked quietly village. Cool dew soaked through Avrahami's shoes as he carried a small spade and hoe across his shoulders. The tools felt heavy, but today he was determined to prove that he was old enough to help.

The day before, the villagers had gathered to hear an important message from Abba Yosi. He told them that while learning Torah beside the river, he had resteded peacefully in its waters.

“For many years I have lived here,”

the spirit explained. “I have never harmed anyone. But now, an evil spirit is coming to drive me away.

If it succeeds,

bring harm to everyone who comes near this river.”

“What can we do?” Abba Yosi asked.

“Gather the people before sunrise,” the spirit replied. “Tell everyone to bring an iron tool. Stand by the river and watch carefully. When the water begins to swirl, strike the tools together and call out, ‘Didan notzach!’ Do not stop until blood rises upon the water. Then you will know the evil spirit has been defeated.”

Before sunrise the next morning, the people of Tzitor gathered with shovels, hoes, spades, and other iron tools. Fathers brought sons who were old enough to help, and Avrahami proudly walked beside his father toward the river.

As they neared the water, Avrahami noticed something was wrong. The villagers spread out along the riverbank and waited in silence.

Suddenly the water began to ripple. The current twisted and churned, and the dark river slowly rose before their eyes.

“Now!” shouted Abba Yosi.

At once, the villagers sprang into action. Shovels crashed against spades, hoes struck rakes, and the ringing sound of iron echoed across the valley. Avrahami banged his own tools together with all his strength.

“Didan notzach!” everyone cried.

Again and again they shouted without stopping. The river churned more violently until, to Avrahami's amazement, a single drop of blood rose to the surface.

The evil spirit had been defeated, and the people of Tzitor returned home praising Hashem for protecting them.

Many years later, after the victory of Hey Teves, the Rebbe explained that this midrash contains an important lesson for every Yid:

Instead of fighting an evil spirit by a river, we fight the Yetzer Hara, who tries to distract us from learning Torah, doing mitzvos, and serving Hashem.

And just as the people of Tzitor triumphed over the spirit by listening carefully to Abba Yosi, we can also be victorious by following the Rebbe's hora’os.

The Rebbe requested that Chassidim begin preparing for Yud Shvat already in Teves, 30 days before. We do this by making good hachlatos and choosing a mashpia to guide us, just like the Yidden in Tzitor had Abba Yosi to guide them. Our mashpia should test us on our progress three times before Yud Shvat.

When we follow the Rebbe's instructions and continue fighting the Yetzer Hara, we can confidently sing:

Didan notzach—victory is ours!

The Seventy-Two Rooms 8 Teves, 3515 (Just over 100 years before the Chanuka miracle)

It’s Asara B’Teves. Everyone bends over their siddurim, saying selichos in low, serious voices. Line by line, they remember the tragedies that happened to the Yidden in the month of Teves.

write the Torah in Greek.”

When was the Torah translated to Greek? And why is that sad enough to mention in selichos?

*** More than two thousand years ago, the powerful King Talmai (Ptolemy) ruled over Mitzrayim and Yavan (Greece).

He had wealth, power, and a vast empire. But what he loved most was his enormous library, filled with books and scrolls from around the world.

Yet, one book was missing: the Torah.

“I want the Torah in my library,” King Talmai declared. “But it’s in Hebrew, and I can’t understand it. I must have it translated into Greek!”

When a king gives an order, no one dares to refuse. “Guards!” he commanded. “Bring me seventy-two of the greatest Jewish sages!”

The officers hurried to obey. Soon, seventy-two talmidei chachamim stood before the king.

But King Talmai didn’t tell them why they had been brought there. Before they could speak to one another, he sent each talmid chacham into a separate room. Then, going from room to room, he gave them all the same command: “Translate the Torah into Greek!”

The doors closed, and each sage began to write.

But soon, they all realized the same problem: In thirteen places, a correct translation could cause King Talmai to misunderstand the Torah. They would have to change the words to express the Torah's true meaning.

But what if each talmid chacham made different changes? What if the translations didn’t match? King Talmai would be furious!

There was no way to know what the others were writing. They each had to decide on their own.

Finally, on Ches Teves, the translations were finished.

“Lay out the scrolls and compare them!” King Talmai ordered.

The guards obeyed. To the chachamim's amazement, every translation was identical. All seventy-two chachamim had made the exact same thirteen changes!

But surprisingly, the chachamim didn't celebrate. They saw this as one of the saddest days in Jewish history—as tragic as the day the Yidden made the Eigel Hazahav.

Why? After such a great neis, what was so sad?

Chazal didn’t compare the translation to bowing to the Eigel. They compared it to the day that the Eigel was made.

On that day, no one had worshipped it yet. But what had been created? The possibility for the aveira to happen later.

The same was true on Ches Teves. The chachamim had translated the Torah carefully, and Hashem even made a neis to protect them.

But still, they saw what could happen later. Now that the Torah was available in Greek, anyone could learn it anywhere. Instead of being taught in an environment of warmth and kedusha by teachers with Yiras Shamayim, it could be misunderstood and even misused. This possibility is what made Ches Teves such a sad day.

We can learn from this, too. Sometimes, things seem fine at first—a new book, an exciting game, a funny comment.

But a Yid stops and thinks: Where could this lead? Will it still be good later?

Alex was about to leave, but then he stopped.

After moving on shlichus, Tatty and Mommy were excited to see how many young families lived in our neighborhood. They immediately opened a Jewish Kids Club, and many children came.

A few months later, Tatty and Mommy began thinking bigger. “Let’s open a Hebrew school for next year!” they decided.

It was a great idea, but there was a big challenge: A Hebrew school would need to be in a proper school setting for families to feel comfortable sending their kids. But our shlichus was still new, and renting another space didn’t feel possible yet.

Tatty and Mommy kept coming back to the idea, but it just didn’t seem like it could work.

At that time, Tatty had a monthly Sunday program called “BLT”—Bagels, Lox, Torah, and Tefillin. Men would come to enjoy breakfast, learn Torah, and put on tefillin.

One Sunday, Tatty finished setting up early. Seeing that he had some time until the men would show up, he sat down to write to the Rebbe: We want to open a Hebrew school, he wrote. Please give us a bracha to find a beautiful space, either free or for a very low price.

He finished writing his letter, and the men began to arrive. One of them was new. His name was Alex.

After the program ended, Alex stayed behind. “Rabbi, I’m worried,” he said quietly. “My kidneys aren’t working properly, and I’ve been very sick for almost two years. I need a kidney donor—someone who can give me a healthy kidney—but it’s very hard to find one. I’m getting weaker and weaker, and I don’t know what will be.”

Tatty listened with compassion. He spoke to Alex about bitachon, and how even in hard situations, a Yid trusts that Hashem will help.

Alex thanked Tatty and then turned to leave. Suddenly, he stopped.

“Rabbi,” he said, turning back around, ““I’m a developer, and I just finished building a new Montessori preschool about five minutes

Tatty could hardly believe his ears!

Alex took Tatty to see the building, and showed him large classrooms that had their own separate entrance. “You can use this space for free,” he said.

For free?! That was exactly what Tatty had asked the Rebbe for just a few hours earlier!

Of course, Tatty accepted Alex’s generous offer. Thanks to that beautiful space, forty-six children joined our Hebrew school in its first year! And that was only the beginning. For the next six years, we used the building for Hebrew school and many other programs as well.

Tatty continued to help Alex put on tefillin each week. Then, just two months after that first BLT, Alex called with incredible news. “Rabbi, the doctors found a kidney donor!”

Alex asked Tatty to come to the hospital before the surgery and help him put on tefillin. Baruch Hashem, the procedure was successful, and Alex put on tefillin the next day to thank Hashem.

Since then, Alex has been putting tefillin on every day!

When Tatty wrote to the Rebbe about our Hebrew school, the brachos brought more good than he ever could have imagined.

Our Hebrew school got a beautiful home, where many Jewish children came to learn Torah and do mitzvos. Alex grew closer to Yiddishkeit and got the kidney transplant he so desperately needed.

And it all started with a letter to the Rebbe.

The beautiful space continued helping our shlichus grow. For six years, we used it for Hebrew School, children’s programs, shiurim, and many other events. By then, baruch Hashem, our community had grown so much that we were able to open our own Chabad House!

The Poisonous Plot Cairo, Egypt

Throughout Cairo and the surrounding lands, the Rambam was famous as both a great talmid chacham and a brilliant doctor. So when the sultan chose him to be his personal doctor, everyone was happy.

I used to be the sultan’s doctor, Hakim fumed. Now nobody thinks I’m important, all because of the Rambam!

Each day, Hakim grew more jealous. I must get rid of him, he thought.

Soon, Hakim thought of a wicked plan.

He rushed to the palace and bowed low before the sultan. “Your Majesty,” he declared. “I have discovered that the Rambam is planning to poison you!”

The sultan gasped. “How could that be?”

“I will prove it.” Hakim’s eyes flashed. “Tell both of us that someone is trying to poison you, and order us to prepare a medicine that will save your life.

“All doctors know,” the evil man continued, “that a stronger poison can stop a weaker poison from working. The honest doctor will bring the strongest poison possible, because he wants to save you. But the one who is really plotting against you will bring a weaker poison, so that the poison in your food will still work.”

The sultan narrowed his eyes. “How will I know whose poison is stronger?”

“We will do a little test,” Hakim said, his smile widening. “I will drink the Rambam’s poison first, and then my own. If I live, it will show that my poison is stronger. Then the Rambam will drink mine, and then his own. If he dies, you will know that his poison was weaker, and that he was the one plotting against you.”

The sultan agreed to the plan. The next day, he called both doctors to the palace and told them about the dangerous test.

“But Your Majesty,” the Rambam said, “If

Hakim drinks my poison, he will die.”

Hakim grinned. “I’m not afraid.”

As the Rambam rode home, he wondered why Hakim looked so smug. Surely Hakim knew that the Rambam could prepare a stronger poison. What trick was he hiding?

But at home, there was no more time to wonder. His waiting room was full of patients and people with Torah questions. The Rambam helped each one, then davened ma’ariv, learned, and wrote late into the night.

Only when he lay down to rest did the Rambam understand Hakim’s plot. I know what to do, he thought.

The next morning, after davening and learning, the Rambam prepared a mixture of red wine and water. Then, he rode to the palace.

Hakim was already there, a sly smile on his face.

At the sultan’s signal, the two doctors exchanged bottles and drank both mixtures.

For a few moments, no one moved. Suddenly, Hakim cried out in pain and fell to the floor, dead.

“Your Majesty,” the Rambam said, “I didn’t kill Hakim. His own plan killed himself.”

“What do you mean?” The sultan asked in amazement.

“You see,” the Rambam explained, “Hakim drank a slow poison before coming to the palace. Then he gave me a harmless drink, expecting me to bring a strong poison. He thought my poison would save him, but would make me die.

“I realized his trick, so I also brought a harmless mixture. Since Hakim never received the poison he was counting on, the slow poison he had already taken caused him to die.”

The sultan laughed in amazement. “Rambam, you are not only the greatest doctor. You are also the wisest of men! From now on, you will be my advisor, as well.”

Indeed, the Rambam faithfully served the sultan as both royal doctor and advisor. Yet, despite the honor, he stayed humble; helping the sick, teaching Torah, and writing the sefarim that continue to guide Yidden today.

Lubavitch House was full of memories, but it was getting too small. What should the shluchim do?

My elter zeidy, Rabbi Moshe Feller, is the head shliach of Minnesota.

In the early years of his shlichus, Chabad of Minnesota bought a big mansion that became known as Lubavitch House.

Hundreds of Shabbatons, weddings, brissim, and programs took place there. Bais Chana for women was there too, bringing thousands of students through its doors to learn Torah and grow in Yiddishkeit.

But almost thirty years later, the building needed a lot of repairs. And by then, Lubavitch House wasn’t big enough to host all the programs, anyway.

“What should we do?” the shluchim wondered. “Should we renovate Lubavitch House? Or should we find a larger building?”

It wasn’t an easy decision. Lubavitch House was very special to them because of the many mitzvos and memories that had happened there. But they also needed a bigger space.

On Erev Rosh Hashana (1999), my elter zeidy came to Lubavitch House and saw a note by the door.

“I’m a contractor,” the note said, “and I love this mansion. I would like to buy it.”

When Elter Zeidy called him, the contractor offered a very large amount of money— almost double what the building was worth!

It now seemed like a good option to sell Lubavitch House. But if they sold it, where would they go? The shluchim searched for a new place, but nothing seemed like the right fit.

On Chol Hamoed Sukkos, Elter

Zeidy called a meeting

senior shluchim. They discussed every detail but still didn’t know what to do.

“We must write to the Rebbe,” they finally decided.

Because it was so urgent, my elter zeidy wrote a letter that same day. Could we sell Lubavitch House? he asked. And if yes, where should we go?

He then faxed the letter to the Ohel.

The next morning, after davening in the Chabad House, a real estate agent who had been helping them came over to my elter zeidy.

“Rabbi Feller,” he said, “you won’t believe this! A perfect building just became available. It has twenty bedrooms, a large dining room, and a huge kitchen. It’s only about ten minutes away from here. The owners have to sell it quickly, so you’d be able to buy it at a low price!”

Elter Zeidy was so excited! The shluchim hurried to see the building, and they all agreed: it was exactly what they needed.

The timing was incredible. Less than twenty- four hours after writing to the Rebbe, the perfect building had become available!

They sold Lubavitch House, and with that money, together with a generous donation, they were able to buy the new building.

From my elter zeidy’s story, I learned that when a Chossid has a question, he shouldn’t feel stuck. Through strengthening our hiskashrus and writing to the Rebbe, we can be sure that the Rebbe will find a way to answer.

The Old Photo

Parshas Shemos
Print PDF

Many years before our shlichus, the Rebbe’s bracha had already begun.

“You won’t believe what I just heard,” Tatty told Mommy one day. “There’s a big, beautiful property for sale right here in Olympia!”

They could already imagine it: shiurim, farbrengens, and children’s programs, with Yidden coming and going. A real home for our Chabad House.

Tatty and Mommy raised money for the down payment, but getting a bank loan was harder. The bank needed a guarantor— someone who would promise to pay if Tatty couldn’t.

As the closing deadline came closer, Tatty wrote to the Rebbe for a bracha. Then he met with supporters to see if they could help. But when the meeting ended, he still had no guarantor.

How would they get the bank loan?

Right then, his phone pinged. It was a message from Dr. K.

Dr. and Mrs. K. live far away in California, but they support our Chabad House because their daughter lives here.

Tatty opened the message. “Amazing news!” he exclaimed. “Dr. K. agreed to be the guarantor!”

Baruch Hashem, we bought the property. But we lived an hour’s walk away, so we would need to move closer.

Then, a few days later, the house near the property went up for sale!

The Rebbe encouraged shluchim to buy homes to show that they’re there to stay, so Tatty and Mommy decided to buy it. They raised money, and once again, Dr. and Mrs. K. helped.

Our shlichus was growing, but so were our expenses. It was hard for Tatty and Mommy to cover the bills.

One day, Tatty got a message from Dr. K. We’re coming to visit our daughter. Can we have a meeting?

Uh oh. Tatty’s heart began to pound. Were they upset? Would they stop helping our Chabad House?

Before the meeting, Tatty wrote a heartfelt letter to the Rebbe. Please give us a bracha that everything should work out in the best way, Tatty wrote.

At the meeting, Dr. K. leaned forward. “Chabad rabbis always tell miracle stories about the Rebbe,” he said. “Now I have one of my own.”

Tatty looked at him in surprise. Dr. K. had

never met the Rebbe. What story did he have?

Dr. K. began: “My wife and I got married about fifty years ago. For a long time, we waited and waited for children. We went to the best doctors, but nothing helped. Then, soon after moving to Zaire, Africa, my wife became pregnant with our daughter—the one who lives here now! Later, we were also blessed with a son.

“For years, we wondered how that miracle happened. And now we know!”

Tatty held his breath. “What changed?”

“Recently, the Chabad rabbi where I live showed me an old photo from Zaire in (1984),” Dr. K. said. “It was found in a collection of pictures sent to the Rebbe years ago. My wife was in the photo! On the back, it said that she lit Shabbos candles and kept some mitzvos.

“But the most surprising thing was the date. The photo was taken one month before my wife became pregnant! I immediately understood that the Rebbe had seen the picture and blessed us with children.”

Tatty sat still in his seat, too amazed to speak.

“Who knows,” Dr. K. added with a smile. “Maybe the Rebbe blessed us with a daughter so that one day she would live in Olympia, and we’d be able to help your Chabad House! Well, let me tell you: I’ll continue my support for as long as I can!”

Baruch Hashem, Dr. K. kept his word and continued to support our Chabad House. And the brachos didn’t stop there. Soon afterward, Tatty saw more help with the finances, and paying the bills became much easier.

He had been so worried about our financial situation, and the Rebbe sent a clear message: Long before our family moved on shlichus, the Rebbe’s brachos had already begun.

Operation Neshek - My Candles!

Parshas Shemos
Print PDF

Baila Brikman

Operation Neshek

Bnos Menachem’s fourth graders headed to the subway station with a bounce in their steps. It was Friday, and that meant one thing: mivtzoim!

Each group was going to a different location with its own madrichos. Our sister Malka Bracha was a madricha for Group 5.

At the station, they made a rally and said pesukim. Soon, the familiar screech of the subway filled the air. Their train sped down the tracks, slowed to a stop, and opened its doors.

Malka Bracha’s group got on, and soon enough, they were at their usual mivtzoim spot—a bike path near Prospect Park.

The girls stood near the path with Shabbos candles in their hands. “Excuse me, are you Jewish?” they asked women and girls who passed by.

But it wasn’t easy.

Bikers zoomed by. Joggers hurried past. Everyone seemed to be in a rush. The girls had just a few seconds to get their attention before they were already gone.

Soon, a little girl came riding by on her scooter with her nanny walking beside her. Instead of rushing past, she came over to say hello.

“Is she Jewish?” the girls asked the nanny.

“Yes, she is,” the nanny said with a smile. “Her name is Noa.”

“I’m four!” Noa added proudly, happy to meet new friends.

The girls gave Noa a special princess-themed package of Shabbos candles.

The nanny smiled. “Her mother already lights.”

“These are for Noa,” the girls explained. “She can light Shabbos candles, too!”

Noa’s face lit up. Her very own Shabbos candles! And they were princess- themed; her favorite!

From then on, Noa came to that spot every Friday. As soon as she noticed the girls down the path, she would race over on her scooter. “My candles!” Noa would call.

Seeing Noa became the highlight of their week.

After some time, the girls decided to prepare something special for her. On their way to the subway station, they stopped at Empire Kosher to choose treats for a Shabbos party package.

They packed candy, a picture of the Rebbe, a candlestick, and a pretty candle-lighting guide into a pink drawstring bag. They couldn’t wait to give Noa her gift. They knew she would love it!

At the subway station, they gathered for their usual rally, with Group 8 joining them for pesukim. Soon they were on the train, listening to a story about chassidim who spent Shabbos in a gas station.

Before they knew it, they were at the bike path.

One of the first people they met was a jogger, hurrying down the path. She slowed down just long enough to take Shabbos candles and then hurried on.

The girls smiled at each other. “Joggers never stop for long,” one girl said. “They don’t want to slow down!”

“Just like us,” another girl laughed. “We’re always on the move with mivtzoim!”

A few minutes later, they saw Noa heading their way.

Noa’s eyes lit up when she saw the gift. “For me?!” she squealed with delight. “Thank you!”

Noa was about to skip away, but then she stopped. “Can I also have candles for my little sister Ray?” she asked. “She’s two! And wait, also for my grandma. She’s coming today! And you know who else I need for? My cousin Sophie. She likes to do whatever I do!”

“Of course!” the girls exclaimed. They were thrilled that Noa was helping so many others light Shabbos candles.

the bike path, almost expecting to see her scooter racing toward them and hear her happy voice calling, “My candles!”

Noa continued coming every week, and one mitzvah followed the next. The girls signed her up for Ois B’sefer Torah, and they prepared packages to give her before each yom tov. And when her bubby and aunt were coming to visit, Noa made sure to get candles for them, too.

But Noa’s story gave them a new excitement for their weekly mivtzoim. Now, every time they give Shabbos candles to a Jewish woman or girl, they remember what they saw with their own eyes: One mitzvah leads to another, and that light can keep spreading until the whole world shines with Torah and mitzvos!

But one week, Noa didn’t come. Is everything okay? Malka Bracha texted the nanny.

This week, let’s go on mivtzoim and give Shabbos candles to a Jewish woman or girl. One mitzvah sparks another. You never know how far that light will go!

Noa’s school ends later now, the nanny texted back, So we won’t be on the bike path at the same time anymore. She’ll miss you!

How Can We Do the Impossible?

Parshas Vaeira

When was the last time someone asked you to do something and you said, “I can’t”?

When Hashem commands Moshe Rabbeinu to speak to Paroh, Moshe replies, “I can’t.” He worried that his poor speech would stop him from doing a good job.

Moshe represents kedusha and Paroh represents kelipa. When Moshe says that he can’t speak to Paroh, Moshe means that he doesn’t think he has the ko’ach to overcome the evil of kelipa.

That’s why Hashem gives Moshe a special power: “I have made you a master over Paroh.”

Moshe gets this special power because he is the nasi hador, the leader of the generation. And when the Yidden are connected to Moshe, this special power is passed along to them, too.

How can a chayol overcome something very hard?

By trying harder on their own.

By connecting to the power that Hashem passed down to our “Moshe”, the Rebbe.

Hashem told Moshe, “Look, I have

Until Moshiach comes, the Yetzer Tov and the Yetzer Hara battle within each of us. If the Yetzer

Hara starts to win, the neshama feels more and more distant from Hashem. It can seem like the neshama has no way to succeed. This is where Moshe Rabbeinu’s special power comes in.

In every generation there is a “Moshe,” a nasi hador. The Rebbe is our nasi. He has that same power from Moshe. When we connect to the Rebbe, this power is given to us, since every Yid has a spark of the nasi inside. Through this we can conquer the Yetzer Hara.

Armed with this ko’ach from the Rebbe, we can accomplish hard things—even things that seem impossible. And with this ko’ach, we will win over the darkness of Golus once and for all!

How do we see that the power of Moshe was successful in overcoming the power of Paroh?

(For example, “I can’t give tzedaka because I don’t have a lot of money.) Then, the adult chooses one child to receive an extra hiskashrus boost—the special strength we receive from connecting to our Rebbe.

Both kids are serving Hashem, but one has a special hiskashrus power. Spot the 6 differences.

The Law Changed

Parshas Vaeira
Print PDF

Our preschool was ready to grow, but a public hearing could stop everything.

Inspectors swept through our house, opening doors and checking every room. Tatty followed close behind, waiting nervously for their decision.

Finally, one inspector turned to him with a smile.

“Congratulations,” he said. “Your home passed the inspection. You have permission to open your preschool! For the first year, you may have eight students.”

Tatty and Mommy were thrilled. Soon, our home was filled with the happy sounds of children playing, learning alef-beis, and singing the words of davening.

The next year, Tatty and Mommy wanted to accept more kids into the preschool. But there was a challenge: They would need a new permit.

Tatty began filling out the forms, but it got complicated.

“Since you want more than eight children, your preschool will no longer be considered a small home daycare,” a worker explained. “To have a larger daycare, you will need to change the zoning of your house. That takes special permission.”

Then she added, “We’ll send letters to all of your neighbors telling them about your plans. If anyone objects and says they don’t want a large preschool on your block, there will be a public court hearing to decide if you should get the new permit or not.”

Tatty’s heart sank. At a public hearing, people could try convincing the city not to let our preschool grow.

Still, there was no other way to receive permission. Tatty gave in the forms and hoped for the best.

A short time later, a letter arrived. A neighbor objected, it said. A public hearing will be scheduled.

There was nothing that Tatty and Mommy could do. They tried staying hopeful, but it was hard. Our preschool was ready to grow, and more

Jewish children were waiting to come. But now, one neighbor’s objection could stop everything!

Tatty traveled to the Ohel and wrote a long letter to the Rebbe. Please give us a bracha to receive the permit easily, without any trouble, Tatty davened.

Arriving back home, Tatty waited anxiously to find out when the public hearing would take place. Every time he got an email, he hurried to check it. But no updates came.

Then one day, a nearby shliach sent him good news:

A new law called SB-234 was just passed in California, he wrote. It changes the rules for home daycares. Under the new law, you will no longer need special zoning to make your daycare larger!

Tatty could hardly believe it.

“Guess what?” he called to Mommy. “We won’t need a public hearing!”

Tatty submitted a new application, and everything went smoothly. There were no letters to the neighbors, no objections, and no hearing. Baruch Hashem, the permit was approved, and our preschool was able to welcome more children.

Tatty had asked the Rebbe for a bracha to receive the permit easily and without any trouble. The answer came in an incredible way: the law itself had changed!

It had to be repeated many times before the crowd grasped it. Over the years, it was often sung at farbrengens.
The Rebbe requested that this niggun be sung by all the campers and staff at the special farbrengen held in Gan Yisroel NY (Swan Lake) in תשי״ז‎ (1957).

The Last Escape Room

Mendel and Sara Shir have just finished turning the newly- renovated garage into an escape room. Their younger siblings must find the clues and figure out which niggun to sing in order to leave the room. Freidel, Tzvi, and Yossi enter.

Click. The door closes behind them.

“Hey!” Tzvi says. “Where are the clues?”

“Yes, the garage is empty! There’s not even an old sefer on the shelves!” says Freidel.

So may I look for You in the Mikdash

“And no Rebbe picture or pushka on the walls!” says Yossi.

“Why is there a steam machine in the corner? It’s too hot.” complains Tzvi.

Freidel sneezes. “It’s dusty too.”

The door opens. “You figured it out!” says Mendel. “This niggun is about how Golus is like being locked up in a hot, dry place, far from Hashem. Our neshamos cry for Hashem to take us out. And just like we opened the door for you, Hashem will open the door for all of us, to the Geula Shelaima!”

Yossi starts to kvetch. “I’m thirsty!”

Crying in a hot, dusty, empty room? Tzvi has a thought.

“Tzama lecha nafshi...” he sings.

“That was a scary room!” exclaims Yossi, as he accepts the iced tea and chocolate cookies that Sara has waiting for them. “I’m glad we’re out!”

Rebbe Story

One Year Later

Parshas Bo
Print PDF

Bubby and Zeidy traveled to the Ohel with a heartfelt request.

Soon after our bubby and zeidy got married, Bubby needed surgery.

Baruch Hashem, she recovered. But afterward, the doctors explained that the surgery had caused permanent damage. It would now be very hard for her to have children.

For the next three years, Bubby and Zeidy never gave up hope.

They davened and tried everything the doctors suggested. They wrote to the Rebbe often, asking for a bracha.

But time kept passing, and they still didn’t have children.

At the time, Bubby and Zeidy were on shlichus in Argentina. Sometimes, when they traveled, they would stop in New York and go to the Ohel.

But it was always just a stopover along the way. It was never a special trip of its own.

As Yud Shvat, (1998) came closer, Bubby and Zeidy had an idea.

“Let’s travel to the Rebbe,” they decided. “We won’t visit anywhere else. We’ll go only to ask for the bracha that we want so much.”

On Vov Shvat, they landed in New York and went straight to the Ohel.

Bubby and Zeidy stayed in Crown Heights for a few weeks, returning to the Ohel at every possible opportunity.

“Rebbe, please bentch us with children," they davened.

When they returned to Argentina, Bubby and Zeidy began preparing for a new medical treatment that was suggested to them.

After a few tests, the specialist called with disappointing news.

“I’m sorry,” he said. “The treatment won’t work this time. It’s not possible for you to

have a baby right now. You’ll have to wait a few months and try again.”

Bubby and Zeidy were devastated. After waiting for so long, they had hoped that this treatment would finally help. They didn’t want to wait any longer!

A few weeks later, Bubby started feeling unwell. She went to the doctor to make sure that everything was okay.

The doctor examined her and smiled. “It’s normal for you to be feeling this way,” he told Bubby. “You’re expecting a baby!”

Bubby could hardly believe her ears. The specialist had just told them that the treatment wouldn’t work. And yet, here she was, expecting a child!

Bubby and Zeidy were overjoyed. After more than three years of waiting and davening, they had finally received the wonderful news.

On Vov Shvat, (1999), their first child, my father, was born.

Does that date sound familiar? It was exactly a year after Bubby and Zeidy had traveled to the Ohel!

They had made a special trip to the Rebbe just to daven for their greatest wish. Now, on that very same date, they held their precious baby in their arms, seeing clearly how the Rebbe’s bracha had come true.

“Yankel, please read the next letter,” the melamed said.

Yankel bent over his page. His finger rested on the letter, but his eyes were looking out the window.

The boy blinked. “Uhh … reish?”

The melamed sighed. “It’s a daled.”

He looked around the room. One boy was drawing something in the frost on the window. Another was whispering to the boy next to him. The melamed closed the siddur for a moment and took a deep breath.

These boys weren’t trying to make trouble. They were farm boys. They loved running in the fields, helping their fathers stack the hay, and taking care

The Secret Inside the Trees of the animals. Sitting in cheder was hard for them.

Still, the melamed felt discouraged. If they can barely read the alef-beis, he thought, how will they ever learn Torah?

On Chamisha-Asar B’Shvat, the melamed had a day off. He wrapped himself in his worn coat and walked out of the village toward the forest. How do trees celebrate their Rosh Hashana? he wondered, as the snow crunched under his boots.

He looked at the forest and stopped. The trees were bare. Their branches were covered with thick white snow. They don’t look like they’re celebrating, thought the melamed. They look almost dead.

Just then, a strong wind blew through the trees. The branches swayed and the snow sparkled in the sunlight. To the melamed, the white snow now looked like Yom Kippur talleisim and kittelach, and the wind sounded like whispered tefillos.

He stood very still and listened. Suddenly, everything changed before his eyes.

The melamed could see through the sparkling snow and through the bumpy bark, as if the trees were made of clear glass.

And deep inside the branches, tiny green sprouts were pushing closer to the outside. They hadn’t come out yet, because the world was still too cold. But no doubt, life was stirring. New buds were waiting for the right time to blossom, when Hashem would send warmth and sunshine.

The melamed stared in wonder. “These trees are not dead,” he whispered. “They are full of life inside.”

A gust of wind blew snow into his face. He closed his eyes. When he opened them again, the forest looked back to normal. The trees were still white and bare; no hints of growth in sight.

But the melamed felt uplifted.

As he walked back to the village, he thought about his students.

I only see the outside, he thought. I see boys who mix up daled and reish. I see boys who draw on the windows instead of focusing. But inside every one of them is a neshama. Inside, every one of them has hidden kochos, waiting to bud and blossom.

The next day, Yankel mixed up the letters again. This time, the melamed didn’t sigh. He bent down gently and pointed.

“Look carefully,” he said with warmth. “A daled has a little corner. Try again.”

Yankel looked at the letter. “Daled,” he said.

The melamed smiled. “Very good.”

The Winning Bid

Parshas Beshalach
Print PDF

Zeidy found the perfect campsite, but the deal suddenly fell apart.

Zeidy stood in the middle of a large, empty field.

There was space here to build bunkhouses, a dining room, and everything else that Camp Gan Yisroel of Florida needed. A generous donor was even offering the land for free.

Should I take this land to build a campground? Zeidy wrote to the Rebbe.

It was before Gimmel Tammuz, and the Rebbe gave a clear answer: Only buy a campsite that’s already been built.

So Zeidy continued renting campsites while searching for a ready-built one to buy. But many were too expensive, and others weren’t the right fit.

Years passed. Soon, the high costs of rent left the camp owing a lot of money. We can’t continue like this, Zeidy realized. We need to buy a campsite, or the camp will have to close.

Six months before the summer of (2013), Zeidy heard of a nearby campsite being sold at an auction. He hurried over, and sure enough, it was fully built with everything that Gan Yisroel needed. Maybe this is it! he thought with excitement.

The auction started at $930,000, much less than other campsites. Zeidy offered one million dollars—and his offer was accepted!

Zeidy borrowed funds for the down payment and tried to raise the rest of the money. But many people who had promised to donate in the past couldn’t give in the end. Finally, Rabbi Sholom Ber Lipskar a”h found a donor who gave $500,000, and Zeidy raised another $100,000 from other supporters.

It was now days before the closing, and Zeidy still needed to raise a lot of money. A friend offered to lend him the rest, but the money would only arrive the following week.

“That won’t work,” the owners warned. “If the full payment isn’t here by Friday afternoon, the deal is canceled.”

Friday afternoon came and went. The owners gave back the down payment and canceled the deal.

After Shabbos, Zeidy flew to the Ohel and poured out his heart to the Rebbe, asking for a bracha for the owners to change their minds.

When Zeidy returned to Florida, he discovered what had happened.

Seven non-Jewish groups owned the property. When they heard that it

was being purchased by a Jewish camp, six of them wanted to cancel the deal. But they couldn’t legally do that after the agreement had already been made. Once Zeidy missed the deadline, though, they were able to stop the sale.

Zeidy started looking into other options. He hoped that there would be a way for Camp Gan Yisroel of Florida to open that summer.

Two months after Zeidy davened at the Ohel, the campsite was surprisingly put up for auction again. Zeidy placed another bid, this time for $1.2 million, and his offer was accepted!

Now, everything went smoothly. The donor who had given $500,000 before, now offered $1 million so the campgrounds wouldn’t be lost again. And Baruch Hashem, Zeidy quickly raised the rest of the money.

Before long, the keys were finally in his hands.

Zeidy drove straight to the campsite. “What changed?” he asked the manager.

“You won’t believe it,” the manager replied. “Other buyers offered more money. But this time, all seven organizations voted to accept your offer! I don't know what happened!”

Zeidy was filled with awe as he realized the tremendous bracha that had taken place. The same owners who hadn’t wanted to sell the campsite to a Jewish buyer now chose Gan Yisroel, even though others offered more money!

There was no other way to explain it. It was truly a miracle.

We learn from Zeidy what to do when we feel stuck: keep following the Rebbe’s hora’os, even when it’s hard. And when something seems impossible, ask for a bracha and trust that the Rebbe will find a way!

A Home for Chabad of Prescott

Parshas Yisro
Print PDF

Nothing seemed to be working out. Would we ever have a proper Chabad House?

Our family is on shlichus in Prescott, Arizona. When our parents first came to Prescott, they rented a house to live in. Because they didn’t own a big Chabad House yet, they hosted programs in the house and in other places around town.

In 5775 (2015), someone donated a lot of money—enough to buy a Chabad House!

Tatty and Mommy began searching for just the right building in just the right spot. A few months later, they found the perfect building.

Unfortunately, there was a problem. The owner wanted an enormous amount of money, a lot more than Tatty and Mommy could pay. Tatty offered a lower price, but the owner wouldn’t hear of it.

Tatty asked his friends what to do, but their answers confused him. “Borrow money from the bank so you can buy it,” some friends advised. Others, however, thought differently. “Don’t go into debt!” they warned, “it’s not worth it.”

All this back and forth made Tatty’s head spin. Looking for some clarity, he sat down to write a letter to the Rebbe. I’m confused, he wrote. People are giving me opposite pieces of advice. Rebbe, what should I do?

A short while later, Tatty heard that the owner of the building was planning to sell it to someone else. Okay, he thought. It must be hashgacha pratis that we’re not meant to buy it.

But in the end, that deal didn’t work out. The building was put up for sale again.

As soon as he heard this, Tatty wrote another letter to the Rebbe, this time asking for a bracha. Then, he called his real estate agent. “Can you tell the owner that we want to buy it?”

The agent passed on the message, but the owner didn’t respond.

A month later, Tatty got a letter from the owners of the house we were renting. When he opened it up, his heart sank. Your lease is up in 40 days, the letter said. We don’t want to

continue renting the house anymore. You will have to find somewhere else to live.

“What?!” Tatty exclaimed. “How will we find a different place to live in so little time?” With a heavy heart, he sat down and wrote to the Rebbe again. Is this a sign that we should buy the building, no matter the cost?

Exactly ten minutes later, Tatty’s phone rang. It was the real estate agent!

“Great news!” the agent said. “The owner is ready to sell the building to you—at the original low price you offered!”

Tatty and Mommy were thrilled! That very day, they went into contract for the building. The deal moved quickly, and on the day we needed to move out of our house, we got the keys to the building.

Thanks to the Rebbe’s brachos, Chabad of Prescott finally had a home.

"That’s a sign that Moshiach’s mamesh almost here," says Tzvi, grinning back.

"Yeah!" Sara grins. “We used their own language to talk about Hashem—and that’s powerful!

the ªpªthetic vs.

Recon Mission

Getting to know the enemy’s weapons and tactics before planning

In a war, the first step toward victory is to expose the enemy’s strategy. This way, we avoid falling into his trap. In Tzivos Hashem we face the trickiest enemy: the Yetzer Hara.

Here’s his strategy: First, the Yetzer Hara plants negative thoughts in our heads. Then, those thoughts grow into worse

feelings that can lead to even more dangerous actions.

One of the ways the Yetzer Hara tricks us is by telling us to be apathetic. This means to be detached and uncaring about what’s happening around us (different from ‘'pathetic’, which means ‘in a pitiful or sorry state). The Yetzer Hara’s goal is for us to shut out other people’s feelings and be insensitive. He tries convincing us that if we think of others, there won’t be any space left to feel our own feelings or properly care for ourselves.

Look at the following scene and identify where the Yetzer Hara could influence you to be apathetic towards others, and trigger your thoughts, speech, and actions.
